documents.t: Even with consent management systems in place, issues can arise, such as unreflected consent withdrawals or concerns about personal data use. Data Principals need a clear way to raise grievances and track their resolution.
Consent is not just about asking for a yes or no. It involves understanding what personal data is needed, why it is needed, and giving people control over how their data is used.
When a person withdraws consent or their personal data changes, other systems that hold or process that data may need to know about the change so they can take the appropriate action.

This reference explains who can approve, reject, or revoke a consent, what the Consent Portal shows when there's nothing to do, and which API call sits behind each action. For the consent states and the three consent models (direct, delegated, and co-authorized), see Understanding Consent. Everything below is decided by one thing: whether the person viewing the consent has their own entry in its authorizations list. Model authorizations list The subject is Direct consent Empty The only person who can act. The consent is ACTIVE immediately. Delegated consent Names one or more people other than the subject An observer: they can view it but not act on it. Co-authorized consent Names the subject and at least one other person An authorizer, like everyone else named.

Each authorizer decides only for themself. Every named authorizer's decision is recorded separately. The consent becomes ACTIVE only when all of them have approved, and a single rejection makes it REJECTED. Once you've decided, your buttons disappear, even if the consent is still PENDING because someone else hasn't decided yet. Revoking is different from rejecting. Any named authorizer can revoke a consent once it's ACTIVE, not only the one who approved it. Administrators can revoke, but never approve or reject on someone else's behalf. They can revoke a consent that is PENDING or ACTIVE, from Administration → All Consents. REVOKED and EXPIRED are final. They override any earlier per-authorizer decision. Who's viewing Approve / Reject Revoke Subject of a direct consent Nothing to approve; it's already ACTIVE Yes, while ACTIVE Subject of a delegated consent No No A named authorizer (in a delegated or co-authorized consent, including the subject of a co-authorized consent) Yes, until they've decided, while PENDING Yes, while ACTIVE Administrator, under All Consents No Yes, while PENDING or ACTIVE

documents.t: Action Request Token Approve POST /api/users/v1/me/consents/{consentId}/authorize with {"state": "APPROVED"} The authorizer's own user token. Self-service calls need only internal_login. Reject POST /api/users/v1/me/consents/{consentId}/authorize with {"state": "REJECTED"} The authorizer's own user token Revoke (self-service) POST /api/users/v1/me/consents/{consentId}/revoke, with no body The subject's or an authorizer's own user token Revoke (administrator) POST /api/identity/consent-mgt/v2.0/consents/{consentId}/revoke, with no body A token with internal_consent_mgt_consent_update The rules in this guide are enforced by the Consent Portal. Identity Server itself accepts an /authorize call in any consent state, so an application calling the API directly must apply the same checks, for example never approving a REVOKED or EXPIRED consent.

documents.t: When there's nothing for you to do, the consent detail page explains why rather than just hiding the button: You'll see this When "Waiting for authoriser approval." You're the subject of a delegated consent, and it's still PENDING. "This consent has been approved." / "...rejected." You're the subject of a delegated consent, and a decision has been made. "You've made your decision. Waiting for the rest to decide." You're a named authorizer who has already approved, and the consent is still PENDING on someone else. "You've rejected this consent." You're the authorizer whose rejection ended it. "This consent has been revoked." / "...expired." The consent has reached a final state, and no further action is possible for anyone.

This reference covers the Event Notification API: topics, subscriptions, publishing, the webhook receiver contract, polling, and completion reports. For the concepts, see Understanding Event Notifications. For a step-by-step walkthrough with the Consent Portal and the sample webhook listener, see Try Out: Event Notifications. For the server settings, see Configure Event Notifications. For every endpoint and schema, see the Event Notification API specification.

The API base URL is: https://<host>:9443/api/dpdp/event-notifications/v1 For a specific tenant, add /t/<tenant-domain> after the port. Topics, subscriptions, events, and deliveries are isolated by tenant, and the tenant always comes from the URL and the token, never from a request body. Scopes: each operation needs one notifications:* scope, listed in Managing Access. The dpdp-consent-admin role holds all eight, but the Consent Portal doesn't request the polling and completion scopes, so a portal token never carries them. Give each publishing or receiving system its own application with only the scopes it needs. The examples use these variables: export API_BASE="https://localhost:9443/api/dpdp/event-notifications/v1" export GROUP_ID="carbon.super" # the tenant domain export ACCESS_TOKEN="<token-with-topic-and-subscription-scopes>" export PUBLISHER_TOKEN="<token-with-notifications:events:write>" export RECEIVER_TOKEN="<token-with-notifications:events:poll-or-event-deliveries:complete>" For a local Identity Server with a self-signed certificate, add -k to a curl command. Never use -k in production; configure a trusted CA, or pass it with --cacert.

The accelerator creates these topics for every tenant when system_topics_auto_create_enabled = true (the default). It publishes to them automatically when lifecycle_events.publishing_enabled = true (the default), so don't publish to them yourself. Topic Published when Carries a purpose? consent.update A consent is updated, or an authorization is approved or rejected Yes consent.revoke A consent or its authorization is revoked Yes consent.expire The expiry reconciler records a consent as expired Yes user.data.change A user's profile claims are updated No user.account.delete A user account is deleted No System topics can't be deregistered. The two user topics also need the dpdpUserLifecycleEventHandler event handler, which configure.sh adds; see Configure lifecycle event publishing.

curl -X POST "${API_BASE}/topics" \ -H "Authorization: Bearer ${ACCESS_TOKEN}" \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{ "name": "delivery.preferences.update", "description": "A customer updated their delivery preferences" }' name is required and must be unique in the tenant. A new topic is active. To list topics, call GET /topics?status=active&limit=20&offset=0. List responses return items and total. To deregister a user topic, call DELETE /topics/<topic-id>. A topic can't be deregistered while any subscription that references it is active, pending, or stale.

A subscription links one or more topics to a purpose filter and a delivery mode: webhook (pushed to a callback URL) or poll (fetched by the receiver). Filter type Matching events all Every event on the subscribed topics specific Events that carry at least one of the listed purposes all_except Events that carry at least one purpose that isn't listed name and delivery.sharedSecret are required for both modes. Store the secret before you submit it; responses never return it. A subscription covers 1 to 100 active topics, fixed at creation. specific and all_except need at least one purpose. Purpose matching is case-insensitive. A subscription that includes user.data.change or user.account.delete must use all, because user events carry no purpose. Any other filter is rejected with 422. A tenant can't mix webhook and poll subscriptions on the same topic, and overlapping webhook subscriptions to the same callback URL are rejected (409).

curl -X POST "${API_BASE}/subscriptions" \ -H "Authorization: Bearer ${ACCESS_TOKEN}" \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{ "name": "CloudEngage - consent changes", "topics": ["consent.update", "consent.revoke"], "filter": { "type": "specific", "purposes": ["marketing-email"] }, "delivery": { "mode": "webhook", "callbackUrl": "https://subscriber.example.com/dpdp/events", "sharedSecret": "<strong-random-secret>" } }' The subscription starts as pending, and becomes active once the callback answers the verification challenge (see Respond to verification). If verification attempts run out, it becomes stale. After fixing the receiver, retry with POST /subscriptions/<subscription-id>/verify, or select Re-verify webhook in the portal. The callback URL must use an allowed port (by default, none or 80, 443, or 8443) and can't point to a private network address unless allow_private_network_callback_targets = true. HTTP callback URLs are allowed by default (allow_http_callback_url = true); set it to false in production so only HTTPS is accepted. See Configure webhook delivery.

curl -X POST "${API_BASE}/subscriptions" \ -H "Authorization: Bearer ${ACCESS_TOKEN}" \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{ "name": "MedExpress - delivery preferences", "topics": ["delivery.preferences.update"], "filter": { "type": "all" }, "delivery": { "mode": "poll", "sharedSecret": "<strong-random-secret>" } }' A poll subscription has no callback URL and is active immediately. Keep the returned subscriptionId and the shared secret; the receiver needs both to poll. To delete a subscription, call DELETE /subscriptions/<subscription-id>, or use the portal. Its status becomes deleted, and its event and delivery history are kept.

Publish to an active user topic with a token that has notifications:events:write: curl -X POST "${API_BASE}/events" \ -H "Authorization: Bearer ${PUBLISHER_TOKEN}" \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -H "group-id: ${GROUP_ID}" \ -d '{ "topic": "delivery.preferences.update", "purposes": ["order-delivery"], "payload": { "customerReference": "cust-0001", "change": "DELIVERY_WINDOW_UPDATED" } }' The group-id header is required. It must equal the tenant domain (carbon.super for the super tenant), because every subscription's group is the tenant domain. An event with any other group ID is stored but reaches no subscriber. purposes is optional. It's what specific and all_except filters match against. The event and its deliveries are created together. Only active subscriptions on the same tenant, group, and topic whose filter matches get a delivery. Keep personal data out of the payload. Send a reference the receiver can look up instead.

Identity Server sends every request for a subscription to its callbackUrl as an HTTP POST: first the verification challenge, then each event delivery. The sample listeners implement this contract, as described in webhook-listener.openapi.yaml.

{ "type": "subscription.verification", "subscriptionId": "<subscription-id>", "topics": ["consent.update", "consent.revoke"], "challenge": "<one-time-challenge>" } When type is subscription.verification, check that topics matches what the receiver expects, then respond with HTTP 200, Content-Type: text/plain, and the exact challenge string as the body. Surrounding whitespace is ignored, but any other content fails verification.

An event delivery has Content-Type: application/json and these headers: Header Description Delivery-Id Stable delivery identifier. Use it to reject duplicates. event-signature sha256=<hex HMAC-SHA256> of the raw request body, made with the subscription's shared secret With payload signing enabled (the default), the body contains only a compact JWS signed with the tenant's key: { "signedPayload": "<base64url-header>.<base64url-claims>.<base64url-signature>" } Its decoded claims look like this: { "iss": "https://localhost:9443/oauth2/token", "sub": "carbon.super", "aud": "dpdp-event-notifications", "iat": 1787651970, "jti": "<delivery-id>", "txn": "<event-id>", "payloadHash": "<HMAC-SHA256 of the embedded payload>", "payload": { "deliveryId": "<delivery-id>", "eventId": "<event-id>", "subscriptionId": "<subscription-id>", "orgId": "carbon.super", "groupId": "carbon.super", "topic": "consent.revoke", "eventPayload": { "consentId": "c7c6b814-ef76-4eb4-9494-8af1b98a9ed1", "previousStatus": "ACTIVE" } } } To verify a delivery: Compute HMAC-SHA256 over the exact raw body bytes with the shared secret, and compare sha256=<lowercase hex> with event-signature in constant time. Don't re-serialize the JSON first. Verify the JWS with RS256 only, using the key whose kid matches the tenant's trusted JWKS endpoint. Keep the issuer-to-JWKS mapping in your own configuration; never fetch keys from a location taken from an unverified token. The super tenant uses /oauth2/token and /oauth2/jwks, without /t/carbon.super. Check iss, sub, aud, and iat. Check that jti, the Delivery-Id header, and payload.deliveryId agree, and that txn matches payload.eventId. Check the expected tenant, group, topic, and subscription, then process payload.eventPayload.

Return a 2xx only after durably accepting the event, for example after committing it to an inbox table or queue. The sender waits up to five seconds, so do the business work asynchronously afterwards. Receiver outcome Response What happens next Verified event committed 202 or another 2xx The delivery becomes delivered. The same delivery was already accepted 2xx Acknowledge it again without repeating the work. Invalid signature, or unexpected tenant or subscription 401 or 403 Retried like any failure; investigate the configuration. Storage unavailable 503 Retried. Every non-2xx response, and every transport failure, is retried. With max_retries = 5, there are at most six attempts, with a backoff of base_backoff_seconds × 3^(retry number - 1). A delivery that runs out of attempts becomes failed. See Retry a failed webhook delivery. Deduplicate by Delivery-Id with a durable uniqueness constraint. A delivery can arrive again after a timeout or recovery, and the body may be signed again on retry, so don't deduplicate by body. Deliveries can arrive out of order. A 2xx proves acceptance, not that the work is done. Make the business effects idempotent, and retry or quarantine failures on your side. To record that the work is done, submit a completion report.

After processing a webhook delivery, a receiver can submit a signed completion report with a token that has notifications:event-deliveries:complete. The signature is an HMAC-SHA256, made with the subscription's shared secret, over: v1
completion
<deliveryId>
<exact-request-body> This binds the report to one delivery. Send the body bytes exactly as signed. DELIVERY_ID="<delivery-id>" SHARED_SECRET="<subscription-shared-secret>" COMPLETION_BODY='{"completionStatus":"completed","completionEvidence":"https://processor.example/evidence/receipt.pdf"}' COMPLETION_SIGNATURE="sha256=$(printf 'v1
completion
%s
%s' "${DELIVERY_ID}" "${COMPLETION_BODY}" \ | openssl dgst -sha256 -hmac "${SHARED_SECRET}" | awk '{print $NF}')" curl -X POST "${API_BASE}/deliveries/${DELIVERY_ID}/completion" \ -H "Authorization: Bearer ${RECEIVER_TOKEN}" \ -H "group-id: ${GROUP_ID}" \ -H "event-signature: ${COMPLETION_SIGNATURE}" \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d "${COMPLETION_BODY}" completionStatus is one of completed, ack, disputed, or partial. completionEvidence is required. It must be an absolute HTTPS URL of up to 512 characters, with no credentials or fragment. completedAt is optional, in epoch milliseconds. A successful report returns 204 No Content. The delivery stays delivered, and the report is shown under Completion Evidence in the portal. Response Cause 401 (EN-4010) Invalid signature, unknown delivery, or group mismatch. All three return the same response, so a caller can't discover whether a delivery exists. 409 (EN-4003) The delivery isn't delivered yet. The sender can still have it in flight briefly after your HTTP response. 409 (EN-4090) A completion report already exists for this delivery.

A poll request is scoped to one subscription. In one call, it can acknowledge deliveries, report errors, and fetch pending deliveries. Long polling isn't supported, so "returnImmediately": false is rejected. SUBSCRIPTION_ID="<poll-subscription-id>" SHARED_SECRET="<poll-subscription-shared-secret>" POLL_BODY='{ "maxEvents": 20, "ack": ["<delivery-id-processed>"], "setErrs": { "<delivery-id-failed>": { "err": "authentication_failed", "description": "Unable to authenticate the signed event" } } }' POLL_SIGNATURE="sha256=$(printf %s "${POLL_BODY}" | openssl dgst -sha256 -hmac "${SHARED_SECRET}" | awk '{print $NF}')" curl -X POST "${API_BASE}/events/poll" \ -H "Authorization: Bearer ${RECEIVER_TOKEN}" \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -H "group-id: ${GROUP_ID}" \ -H "subscription-id: ${SUBSCRIPTION_ID}" \ -H "event-signature: ${POLL_SIGNATURE}" \ -d "${POLL_BODY}" ack lists delivery IDs, and setErrs is keyed by delivery ID, not event ID. A delivery ID can't appear in both. The first poll can have an empty body. Its signature is then calculated over zero bytes, not over {}. An omitted maxEvents uses default_max_events (20). 0 makes an acknowledge-only request, and values above max_events_limit (100) are rejected. The server checks event-signature only when request_hmac_validation_enabled = true (off by default), but sign every request anyway. The response holds pending deliveries in sets, keyed by delivery ID. Each value is a compact RS256 JWS with the same claims as a webhook delivery. Verify it as in Receive and verify deliveries, then acknowledge it in a later poll: { "moreAvailable": false, "sets": { "f5f37c64-6130-4d44-9463-136c8bca4278": "<compact-RS256-JWS>" } }

When a webhook delivery has used all its automatic retries and is failed, fix the receiver and queue it again with a token that has notifications:subscriptions:write: curl -X POST "${API_BASE}/subscriptions/<subscription-id>/events/<delivery-id>/retry" \ -H "Authorization: Bearer ${ACCESS_TOKEN}" The response is 202 Accepted. A delivery that isn't failed with its retries exhausted returns 409.

In the portal, open Event Notifications → Events to see each event's payload and its deliveries, or open a subscription to see its deliveries. The read APIs need notifications:events:read or notifications:subscriptions:read: Operation Method and path List events GET /events Get an event GET /events/{eventId} List deliveries for an event GET /events/{eventId}/deliveries Get a delivery's attempt history GET /events/{deliveryId}/history List deliveries for a subscription GET /subscriptions/{subscriptionId}/events Get a subscription delivery's history GET /subscriptions/{subscriptionId}/events/{deliveryId}

Code Meaning EN-4001 Invalid request, for example a missing group-id or an invalid field EN-4002 A required parameter is missing EN-4003 The resource isn't in a state that allows the operation EN-4010 Invalid signature, or a delivery or group that doesn't match EN-4040 Resource not found EN-4041 Topic not found EN-4042 Delivery not found EN-4043 Event not found EN-4090 The resource already exists, or conflicts with an existing one EN-4220 Webhook verification failed EN-5000 Internal server error EN-5001 The event couldn't be published

Symptom Check Event Notification pages aren't visible in the portal Assign dpdp-consent-admin in the current tenant, then sign in again. 401 or 403 from the API The token must come from the URL's tenant and carry the operation's scope. Get a new token after changing scopes or roles. Subscription creation returns 409 An existing subscription overlaps it: the same callback URL and topics, or the other delivery mode on the same topic. A duplicate name also conflicts. Subscription creation returns 422 A subscription with a user topic must use the all filter. Subscription stays pending or becomes stale The callback must be reachable from Identity Server, on an allowed port, and return the exact challenge with HTTP 200. Then retry verification. A system topic gets no events Check lifecycle_events.publishing_enabled = true and consent_history.enabled = true; consent expiry also needs consent_expiry.enabled = true. User topics need the dpdpUserLifecycleEventHandler event handler. An event is created but has no deliveries The subscription must be active, its topic and filter must match, and group-id must equal the tenant domain. Webhook signature doesn't match Compute the HMAC over the unmodified raw body, not only the nested payload. On macOS, use awk '{print $NF}' with openssl dgst, because LibreSSL prints only the hash.

This reference covers the complaint (grievance) API: its two access surfaces, the requests an application or integration makes, and how to customize complaint emails. For the concepts and the status lifecycle, see Understanding Complaints. For a step-by-step walkthrough in the Consent Portal, see Try Out: Complaints. For every endpoint and schema, see the Complaint Server API specification.

The API has two deliberately separate surfaces under https://<host>:9443/api/dpdp/complaints/v1 (add /t/<tenant-domain> after the port for a specific tenant): Surface Who uses it Scopes What it permits /me/complaints/* The signed-in Data Principal, using their own user token complaints:read:self, complaints:write:self Create, view, and reply to their own complaints, and add public attachments /complaints/* A Data Protection Officer (DPO) or a trusted system complaints:read:any, complaints:write:any Search and manage every complaint in the tenant, add public replies or internal notes, change status, and manage attachments The me surface derives the Data Principal from the token, so never put a userId in a self-service request. A caller asking for someone else's complaint gets 404, with no hint that the ID exists. The dpdp-consent-user role grants the self-service scopes and dpdp-consent-dpo grants the management scopes. dpdp-consent-admin has no complaint scopes. For a system integration, authorize a dedicated application for only the scopes it needs. See Managing Access. A DPO can create a complaint on a Data Principal's behalf through POST /complaints, with the userId in the body, when the complaint arrives by phone, in person, or on paper. Complaints and attachments are isolated by tenant. Use a token issued by the same tenant as the URL. Deadlines, attachment limits, and email notifications are set in deployment.toml. See Configure complaint management. The examples use these variables: export API_BASE="https://localhost:9443/api/dpdp/complaints/v1" export USER_TOKEN="<data-principal-access-token>" export DPO_TOKEN="<dpo-or-integration-access-token>"

List the categories, each with the priority a new complaint in it receives: curl "${API_BASE}/me/complaints/categories" \ -H "Authorization: Bearer ${USER_TOKEN}" The categories are DATA_BREACH, UNAUTHORIZED_DATA_SHARING, CONSENT_WITHDRAWN_DATA_STILL_USED, PURPOSE_VIOLATION, DATA_ERASURE_NOT_COMPLETED, DATA_CORRECTION_NOT_COMPLETED, CONSENT_LIFECYCLE_ISSUE, DATA_ACCESS_DENIED, EXCESSIVE_DATA_COLLECTION, and OTHER. Create the complaint with the Data Principal's own token: curl -X POST "${API_BASE}/me/complaints" \ -H "Authorization: Bearer ${USER_TOKEN}" \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{ "subjectCategory": "CONSENT_WITHDRAWN_DATA_STILL_USED", "description": "I revoked my consent for marketing emails, but I still receive them." }' The response is 201 Created, with the complaint ID, reference ID, priority, status (OPEN), and statutory due date.

Upload evidence as multipart form data. Each file must be a PDF, DOCX, PNG, or JPEG within the configured size limit, and one request can carry up to attachment_max_files_per_upload files (5 by default). The Consent Portal sends one file per upload. Self-service uploads are always public: curl -X POST "${API_BASE}/me/complaints/<complaint-id>/attachments" \ -H "Authorization: Bearer ${USER_TOKEN}" \ -F "file=@incident-screenshot.png;type=image/png" On the management surface, the isPublic part is required and must be sent as text/plain. Without that content type, the value can't be read and the upload is stored as internal: curl -X POST "${API_BASE}/complaints/<complaint-id>/attachments" \ -H "Authorization: Bearer ${DPO_TOKEN}" \ -F "file=@investigation-notes.pdf;type=application/pdf" \ -F "isPublic=false;type=text/plain"

A DPO can post a public reply and change the status in one request: curl -X POST "${API_BASE}/complaints/<complaint-id>/comments" \ -H "Authorization: Bearer ${DPO_TOKEN}" \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{ "message": "We are reviewing your request.", "isPublic": true, "toStatus": "IN_PROGRESS" }' Set "isPublic": false for an internal note. Internal notes and internal attachments never appear on the me surface. Moving a complaint to RESOLVED requires a message describing the outcome. POST /complaints/<complaint-id>/status changes the status without a comment, and takes toStatus and a required note. Every transition is checked against the permitted transitions listed in How status transitions work. A transition that isn't permitted returns 409 (CO-4090). The Data Principal replies through POST /me/complaints/<complaint-id>/comments, with a message and an optional toStatus. When the complaint is WAITING_ON_CLIENT or RESOLVED, the Consent Portal sends "toStatus": "AWAITING_INTERNAL_REVIEW" with the reply. This is how a resolved complaint is reopened. An application on the me surface should do the same. Use GET /me/complaints/<complaint-id>/timeline for the public activity and its attachments, and GET /complaints/<complaint-id>/timeline for the full activity, including internal notes.
documents.s: 4. Reply, add internal notes, and change status

documents.t: Complaint emails are off by default. To send them, set email_notifications_enabled = true and configure the email sender, as described in Configure complaint email notifications. ComplaintCreated, ComplaintCommentAdded, and ComplaintAcknowledged are standard Identity Server notification templates. Edit them per tenant in the Console under Email Templates. Placeholders: {{reference-id}}, {{message-excerpt}}, {{data-principal-name}}, {{actor-name}}, {{category-label}}, {{priority-label}}, {{status-label}}, {{sla-label}}, {{action-url}}, {{recipient-role-label}}, {{headline-html}}, {{footer-text}}, {{action-badge-html}}, {{logo-url}}. A template is written once, when the tenant is first provisioned, and never rewritten, so a Console edit is permanent. The bundled default comes from <IS_HOME>/repository/conf/email/email-dpdp-config.xml. Editing that file needs no rebuild, but only affects tenants provisioned afterward. The file is read once and cached, so restart the server after editing it.

Symptom Check 403 Forbidden The token lacks the operation's scope: complaints:read:self or complaints:write:self on /me/*, and complaints:read:any or complaints:write:any on /complaints/*. After assigning a role, sign in again or get a new token. 404 Not Found on /me The complaint belongs to another user, or the ID is incorrect. 400 when resolving Moving to RESOLVED needs a message (comments) or a note (status endpoint). 409 on a status change The target status isn't permitted from the current status. Attachment rejected Check the file type, the file size, and the number of files in the request against the configured limits. A management upload is internal when it should be public Send the isPublic part as text/plain, for example -F 'isPublic=true;type=text/plain'. No complaint emails email_notifications_enabled is false by default, and the email sender must also be configured.

This section covers the configuration options available for the DPDP Accelerator. All settings are configured in <IS_HOME>/repository/conf/deployment.toml. After making changes, restart WSO2 Identity Server for them to take effect.

Set these values according to your environment: [server] hostname = "<public host name of the Identity Server>" [super_admin] username = "<administrator username>" password = "<administrator password>" create_admin_account = true With the accelerator's user-store configuration, usernames are email addresses. Use an email address for the administrator as well. See the Identity Server documentation on Encrypting passwords with the Cipher Tool to learn how to provide the administrator password as an encrypted secret.

These settings control how consent records are created, updated, and managed: [consent_mgt] enable_v2_api = true revoke_active_consents_on_create = false enable_v2_api — Required for the accelerator. Keep this set to true. revoke_active_consents_on_create — Recommended: false. This prevents a new consent from automatically revoking previously active consents.

By default, the accelerator automatically creates the portal application and roles for each tenant. You only need to change these settings if you want to manage them manually or use your own provisioning logic. [dpdp_accelerator.consent_portal] auto_provisioning_enabled = true client_id = "DPDP_CONSENT_PORTAL" auto_provisioning_enabled = false — Disables automatic provisioning. You will need to create and manage the portal application and the three roles yourself. client_id — The client ID of the DPDP Consent Portal application. If you change it, make sure the same value is configured in the portal's deployment.config.json file at <IS_HOME>/repository/deployment/server/webapps/consent-portal/deployment.config.json. Both values must match for sign-in to work.
documents.s: Configure automatic application and role provisioning

documents.t: The accelerator can automatically provision a sample application for testing consent flows through the REST API. You can use this application with the Try Out flows. [dpdp_accelerator.consent_api_invoker] auto_provisioning_enabled = true client_id = "DPDP_CONSENT_API_INVOKER" To disable it, set auto_provisioning_enabled = false. To find the client secret, go to Console → Applications → DPDP Consent API Invoker → Protocol. Note: Disabling auto-provisioning for the DPDP Consent Portal also disables this provisioning, even when auto_provisioning_enabled is set to true.

You only need to follow these steps if the tenant's automatically provisioned resources are missing or misconfigured. For example, this can happen if the Consent Portal application is deleted or a role's permissions are changed. Make sure auto-provisioning is enabled (see above). In Console, go to Tenant Management, open the affected tenant, and click Update. Saving the tenant again triggers the repair. The accelerator restores any missing resources, including the application, API permissions, and role permissions. Existing roles and their user assignments are not deleted.

Use these settings to control complaint deadlines, attachment limits, and email notifications. [dpdp_accelerator.complaints] statutory_due_period_days = 90 attachment_max_size_bytes = 10485760 attachment_max_files_per_upload = 5 email_notifications_enabled = false statutory_due_period_days — The number of days a complaint can remain open before it is marked as overdue. attachment_max_size_bytes — The maximum allowed size for each attachment. attachment_max_files_per_upload — The maximum number of files in a single upload request to the API. The Consent Portal currently uploads one file at a time. email_notifications_enabled — Enables email notifications for complaints. This is false by default and should only be enabled after configuring email notifications.

Configure these settings if you want to send email notifications for complaints. Email notifications are optional and are not included in the default configuration. Add this section to deployment.toml when you want to enable them. [output_adapter.email] from_address = "abc@gmail.com" username = "abc@gmail.com" password = "<GMAIL_APP_PASSWORD>" hostname = "smtp.gmail.com" port = 587 from_address — The email address shown as the sender. username / password — The credentials used to connect to the SMTP server. For Gmail, use an App Password instead of your regular account password. hostname / port — The SMTP server and port used by your email provider. The example above uses Gmail's SMTP server with port 587. Email notifications are sent when a complaint is created, commented on, or acknowledged. To receive these notifications, the user must also have a Primary Email configured in (Console → User Management → Users)

These settings control how consent changes are recorded and stored for future reference. [dpdp_accelerator.consent_history] enabled = true snapshot_enabled = true enabled = false Disables consent history and the audit trail. snapshot_enabled = false Records that a consent changed, but does not store a full snapshot of the consent at that point in time.
documents.s: Configure consent history and status audit trail

documents.t: The accelerator uses a background job to mark consents as EXPIRED after their expiry date has passed. Consent history must be enabled for this feature to work. [dpdp_accelerator.consent_expiry] enabled = true schedule_mode = "daily" daily_time = "00:00" # timezone = "Asia/Colombo" # interval_seconds = 300 batch_size = 100 max_batches_per_run = 1000 max_run_seconds = 300 schedule_mode — Controls how often the job runs. Use "daily" to run it once a day or "interval" to run it at a fixed interval. For interval mode, set this to "interval" and configure interval_seconds. daily_time — The local time when the job runs. Used only in daily mode, for example, "00:00". timezone — The timezone used to interpret daily_time. If not specified, the server's timezone is used. interval_seconds — The number of seconds between runs. Required when schedule_mode is "interval" and ignored in daily mode. batch_size, max_batches_per_run, max_run_seconds — Control how many consents the job processes in a single run. The default values are suitable for most installations. You can run the job on multiple server instances. The same consent will not be processed more than once.

Event notifications allow other systems to receive notifications when consents or user data change. See the Event Notification Guide for a complete walkthrough of creating topics and subscriptions. [dpdp_accelerator.event_notifications] system_topics_auto_create_enabled = true [dpdp_accelerator.event_notifications.payload_signing] enabled = true audience = "dpdp-event-notifications" system_topics_auto_create_enabled — Automatically creates the five standard topics for each tenant. See Configure lifecycle event publishing for the list of topics. payload_signing.enabled — Signs each event so the receiving system can verify that it was sent by the accelerator. Keep this enabled. payload_signing.audience — The audience value included in the event signature. The receiving system can use it to verify that the event is intended for it.

[dpdp_accelerator.event_notifications.lifecycle_events] publishing_enabled = true publishing_enabled Enables automatic publishing to the five standard topics when a matching event occurs. Set this to false if you want to publish events yourself or disable automatic publishing. The topics remain available even when publishing is disabled. Topic Published when... consent.update A consent's state changes (e.g. approved, a decision recorded). consent.revoke A consent is revoked or withdrawn. consent.expire A consent expires (see consent expiry). user.data.change A user's profile or attributes are modified. user.account.delete A user's account is deleted. user.data.change and user.account.delete also require the following event handler registration. It is enabled by default, so make sure it is still present if you have manually edited deployment.toml: [[event_handler]] name = "dpdpUserLifecycleEventHandler" subscriptions = ["POST_DELETE_USER", "POST_SET_USER_CLAIMS"] The consent.* topics also require consent history to be enabled.

[dpdp_accelerator.event_notifications.polling] default_return_immediately = true default_max_events = 20 max_events_limit = 100 request_hmac_validation_enabled = false default_return_immediately — Keep this true. Long polling isn't supported, so a poll request with "returnImmediately": false is rejected. default_max_events — The default number of events returned in a poll request. max_events_limit — The maximum number of events that can be requested in a single poll. Requests above this limit are rejected. request_hmac_validation_enabled — Requires poll requests to include a signed header that is verified against the subscription's shared secret. Disabled by default.

[dpdp_accelerator.event_notifications.webhook] thread_pool_size = 4 base_backoff_seconds = 5 max_retries = 5 allow_http_callback_url = true allowed_callback_ports = "-1,80,443,8443" allow_private_network_callback_targets = false delivery_worker_batch_size = 50 delivery_worker_poll_seconds = 5 stuck_inflight_threshold_seconds = 10 max_verification_response_body_bytes = 4096 pending_subscription_recovery_threshold_seconds = 60 background_worker_initial_delay_seconds = 10 pending_subscription_recovery_interval_seconds = 30 pending_subscription_recovery_batch_size = 20 worker_shutdown_timeout_seconds = 5 thread_pool_size — The number of webhook deliveries that can be sent concurrently. base_backoff_seconds — The initial wait time before retrying a failed delivery. max_retries — The maximum number of retries for a failed delivery. A value of 5 results in up to 6 delivery attempts in total. allow_http_callback_url — Allows callback URLs that use HTTP instead of HTTPS. Enabled by default; set it to false in production. allowed_callback_ports — The ports that can be used by callback URLs. -1 means a URL with no explicit port. allow_private_network_callback_targets — Allows callback URLs that point to private or internal networks. Enable this only for controlled on-premises environments. delivery_worker_batch_size — The number of pending deliveries a worker processes at a time. delivery_worker_poll_seconds — How often a worker checks for pending deliveries. stuck_inflight_threshold_seconds — How long a delivery can remain in progress before it is considered stuck and retried. max_verification_response_body_bytes — The maximum response size read when verifying a subscription's callback URL. pending_subscription_recovery_threshold_seconds — How long a subscription can remain in pending verification before it is picked up for recovery. background_worker_initial_delay_seconds — How long to wait after server startup before delivery workers start. pending_subscription_recovery_interval_seconds — How often the system checks for subscriptions that are stuck in pending verification. pending_subscription_recovery_batch_size — The number of pending subscriptions recovered in a single check. worker_shutdown_timeout_seconds — How long to wait for in-flight deliveries to complete when the server shuts down. See the Event Notification Guide for more on any of these.
Once you've made the required configuration changes, start the server for them to take effect.

Go to <IS_HOME>/bin and start Identity Server: Linux macOS Windows ./wso2server.sh ./wso2server.sh .\wso2server.bat Continue with Configuring Users and Roles to create users and assign them accelerator roles.

When WSO2 Identity Server starts with the DPDP Accelerator, and whenever a new tenant is created, the accelerator automatically provisions three predefined roles: dpdp-consent-admin, dpdp-consent-dpo, and dpdp-consent-user. This guide walks you through: Creating a new user Understanding accelerator roles Assigning accelerator roles
Follow these steps to create a user in the Identity Server Console.
Open your browser and navigate to the WSO2 Identity Server Console: https://<host>:9443/console Log in with your administrator account (e.g., admin@wso2.com).
documents.s: Step 1: Sign in to the Console

documents.t: In the left navigation sidebar, expand User Management and click Users.
On the top-right of the Users page, click + Add User and select Single User.

Enter the user's details in the Basic Details step: Username (Email): Enter the user's email address (for example, janedoe@wso2.com). Note Under the accelerator's default configuration, usernames are email addresses. First Name: Enter the user's first name (e.g., Jane). Last Name: Enter the user's last name (e.g., Doe). Password Method: Select Set a password for the user and enter a password that meets the displayed complexity requirements (or click Generate). Click Next to proceed. You can optionally assign user groups on the next step or click Next to skip.
documents.s: Step 4: Fill in basic user details

documents.t: On the final Invitation step: Click Close to complete user creation.

The accelerator provides three predefined roles designed to separate user, administrative, and data protection responsibilities: Role Target Persona Key Capabilities dpdp-consent-admin System & Organization Administrators Full oversight over consents, purpose/element catalog management, and event notification subscriptions. Complaint handling is not included; it belongs to dpdp-consent-dpo. dpdp-consent-dpo Data Protection Officers (DPO) Organization-wide complaint inspection, review, internal notes, and complaint resolution without administrative consent privileges. dpdp-consent-user Data Principals / End Users Self-service account deletion (DELETE /scim2/Me), personal complaint filing and tracking, and personal consent history audit views. tip Basic Consent Access: End users can log into the Consent Portal, view their active consents, and authorize or revoke consents without any role assigned. Assign dpdp-consent-user when they need to file complaints, view audit history, or delete their accounts. Role Assignment: dpdp-consent-admin is not automatically assigned to dpdp-consent-dpo. If a user requires both administrative oversight and DPO complaint handling capabilities, assign both roles explicitly. For the scopes each role grants, and the API resource each scope belongs to, see Managing Access.
After creating the user, assign them to the appropriate DPDP role.

In the left navigation sidebar, expand User Management and click Roles. You will see the accelerator's predefined roles: dpdp-consent-admin dpdp-consent-dpo dpdp-consent-user Select the role you want to assign (for example, click the edit icon on dpdp-consent-admin).
In the role details view: Click the Users tab from the top tab menu. Click the + Assign User button.

In the Assign Users dialog: Search for or locate the user (e.g. janedoe@wso2.com). Check the box next to the user's name. Click Save. The user is now assigned to the role and can access the corresponding features in the Consent Portal and APIs.

documents.t: Before setting up the WSO2 DPDP Accelerator, ensure your environment meets the system requirements and dependencies outlined below.

JDK 21 is required. Set JAVA_HOME to the JDK 21 folder and add its bin folder to your PATH. Linux macOS Windows export JAVA_HOME="<JDK_LOCATION>" export PATH=$JAVA_HOME/bin:$PATH java -version export JAVA_HOME="$(/usr/libexec/java_home -v 21)" export PATH=$JAVA_HOME/bin:$PATH java -version $env:JAVA_HOME = "<JDK_LOCATION>" $env:Path = "$env:JAVA_HOME\bin;$env:Path" java -version java -version should report version 21 or later.

A relational database server is required for production and staging environments: Database Supported Versions Usage MySQL 8.0 Production and staging environments PostgreSQL 15, 16, 17 Production and staging environments Embedded H2 Pre-packaged Evaluation, development, and testing only
Download WSO2 Identity Server 7.3.0 and extract the ZIP.

The accelerator needs Identity Server at U2 update level 17 or later. A freshly downloaded Identity Server doesn't include the update tool yet, so get it first: Go to <IS_HOME>/bin and run the setup script. It downloads the update tool that matches your operating system and processor into the same folder: Linux macOS Windows ./update_tool_setup.sh ./update_tool_setup.sh .\update_tool_setup.ps1 In the same folder, run the update tool it downloaded: Linux macOS Windows ./wso2update_linux # ARM64: ./wso2update_linux_arm64 ./wso2update_darwin_arm64 # Intel: ./wso2update_darwin .\wso2update_windows.exe # ARM64: .\wso2update_windows_arm64.exe Self-Updates If the tool reports that it updated itself, run the same command again to update Identity Server. For more information about WSO2 updates and the update tool, see updating WSO2 products.
Once the prerequisites are completed: Continue with Setting Up Servers to install the accelerator and configure server settings.

Complete the Prerequisites first. This section explains how to install the DPDP Accelerator distribution, merge its artifacts into WSO2 Identity Server, and configure the base deployment.toml file. note Ensure the Identity Server is stopped before extracting files, running scripts, or applying configurations.

Download the latest wso2-dpdpiam-accelerator-<version>.zip from the releases page. To build it from source instead, see the repository README. Extract it, and copy the extracted wso2-dpdpiam-accelerator-<version> directory into the root directory of Identity Server <IS_HOME>. The rest of this guide refers to the directories as follows: Directory Placeholder Identity Server <IS_HOME> DPDP Accelerator, inside <IS_HOME> <DPDP_ACCELERATOR_HOME>

Go to <IS_HOME>/<DPDP_ACCELERATOR_HOME>/bin and run the merge script: Linux macOS Windows ./merge.sh ./merge.sh The accelerator's scripts are Bash scripts, so run them from Git Bash or WSL (Windows Subsystem for Linux): ./merge.sh This script copies the accelerator's artifacts—including OSGi bundles, webapps, configuration templates, and database scripts—into their respective directories in <IS_HOME>.

Server-level configurations in WSO2 Identity Server are managed through <IS_HOME>/repository/conf/deployment.toml. The accelerator provides a preconfigured, fully commented template for WSO2 Identity Server 7.3.0: <IS_HOME>/<DPDP_ACCELERATOR_HOME>/repository/resources/wso2is-7.3.0-deployment.toml To apply the configuration: Back up existing configuration: Back up your current <IS_HOME>/repository/conf/deployment.toml file. Copy the template: Copy the accelerator's template to <IS_HOME>/repository/conf/ and rename it to deployment.toml, replacing the existing file: Linux macOS Windows cp <IS_HOME>/<DPDP_ACCELERATOR_HOME>/repository/resources/wso2is-7.3.0-deployment.toml <IS_HOME>/repository/conf/deployment.toml cp <IS_HOME>/<DPDP_ACCELERATOR_HOME>/repository/resources/wso2is-7.3.0-deployment.toml <IS_HOME>/repository/conf/deployment.toml Copy-Item "<IS_HOME>\<DPDP_ACCELERATOR_HOME>\repository\resources\wso2is-7.3.0-deployment.toml" "<IS_HOME>\repository\conf\deployment.toml" info This template contains the baseline settings for the DPDP Accelerator, including datasource definitions, Consent Portal configurations, and event notification settings. Database connection URLs and credentials will be configured in subsequent steps.

If you are using the default keystore provided with the product, it is located at: <IS_HOME>/repository/resources/security/wso2carbon.p12 tip For a production deployment, consider creating a new keystore and configuring it instead of using the default one.

Once the server artifacts are installed and the base deployment.toml template is copied, proceed to configure the databases before starting the server: Continue with Setting up the database to create the required databases and execute the database scripts.

This section explains how to create the required physical databases, populate them with the necessary database scripts, and configure the datasources for WSO2 Identity Server and the DPDP Accelerator. Throughout this guide: <IS_HOME> refers to the root directory of the WSO2 Identity Server 7.3.0 installation. <ACCELERATOR_HOME> refers to the root directory of the extracted DPDP Accelerator distribution.

Create four databases: Database Used by WSO2IDENTITY_DB Identity Server identity and consent data WSO2SHARED_DB Identity Server shared data WSO2AGENTIDENTITY_DB Identity Server AgentIdentity datasource WSO2DPDP_DB DPDP Accelerator data MySQL PostgreSQL Keep the three Identity Server databases on latin1. The shipped Identity Server scripts mix tables that are explicitly latin1 with tables that inherit the database's character set, including in foreign keys, and MySQL rejects those keys if the character sets differ. WSO2DPDP_DB holds multilingual data, so it uses utf8mb4. CREATE DATABASE WSO2IDENTITY_DB CHARACTER SET latin1 COLLATE latin1_swedish_ci; CREATE DATABASE WSO2SHARED_DB CHARACTER SET latin1 COLLATE latin1_swedish_ci; CREATE DATABASE WSO2AGENTIDENTITY_DB CHARACTER SET latin1 COLLATE latin1_swedish_ci; CREATE DATABASE WSO2DPDP_DB CHARACTER SET utf8mb4 COLLATE utf8mb4_0900_ai_ci; Quote the database names. Without quotes, PostgreSQL folds them to lowercase, and the JDBC URLs in datasource configurations that reference WSO2IDENTITY_DB and so on will fail to connect. If you prefer lowercase names, use them consistently everywhere. CREATE DATABASE "WSO2IDENTITY_DB" ENCODING 'UTF8' TEMPLATE template0; CREATE DATABASE "WSO2SHARED_DB" ENCODING 'UTF8' TEMPLATE template0; CREATE DATABASE "WSO2AGENTIDENTITY_DB" ENCODING 'UTF8' TEMPLATE template0; CREATE DATABASE "WSO2DPDP_DB" ENCODING 'UTF8' TEMPLATE template0;

To create the database tables, navigate to the script locations within <IS_HOME>/dbscripts and execute the scripts that correspond to your DBMS against the respective databases. MySQL PostgreSQL Database Script Location WSO2SHARED_DB <IS_HOME>/dbscripts/mysql.sql WSO2IDENTITY_DB <IS_HOME>/dbscripts/identity/mysql.sql WSO2IDENTITY_DB <IS_HOME>/dbscripts/consent/mysql.sql WSO2AGENTIDENTITY_DB <IS_HOME>/dbscripts/identity/agent/mysql.sql WSO2DPDP_DB <IS_HOME>/dbscripts/dpdp-accelerator/complaint/mysql.sql <IS_HOME>/dbscripts/dpdp-accelerator/consent-history/mysql.sql <IS_HOME>/dbscripts/dpdp-accelerator/event-notification/mysql.sql Consent Migration Script For WSO2IDENTITY_DB, execute the consent migration script located at <IS_HOME>/dbscripts/migrations/consent/mysql-migration.txt. For instructions on executing migration scripts, refer to the WSO2 Identity Server Documentation. Database Script Location WSO2SHARED_DB <IS_HOME>/dbscripts/postgresql.sql WSO2IDENTITY_DB <IS_HOME>/dbscripts/identity/postgresql.sql WSO2IDENTITY_DB <IS_HOME>/dbscripts/consent/postgresql.sql WSO2AGENTIDENTITY_DB <IS_HOME>/dbscripts/identity/agent/postgresql.sql WSO2DPDP_DB <IS_HOME>/dbscripts/dpdp-accelerator/complaint/postgresql.sql <IS_HOME>/dbscripts/dpdp-accelerator/consent-history/postgresql.sql <IS_HOME>/dbscripts/dpdp-accelerator/event-notification/postgresql.sql Consent Migration Script For WSO2IDENTITY_DB, execute the consent migration script located at <IS_HOME>/dbscripts/migrations/consent/postgresql-migration.txt. For instructions on executing migration scripts, refer to the WSO2 Identity Server Documentation.

Configure the datasources by following the sample below: MySQL PostgreSQL Open the <IS_HOME>/repository/conf/deployment.toml file and update the datasource configurations: [database.identity_db] url = "jdbc:mysql://<database-host>:3306/WSO2IDENTITY_DB?autoReconnect=true&useSSL=false" username = "<database-user>" password = "<database-password>" driver = "com.mysql.cj.jdbc.Driver" [database.identity_db.pool_options] maxActive = "150" maxWait = "60000" minIdle = "5" testOnBorrow = true validationQuery = "SELECT 1" validationInterval = "30000" defaultAutoCommit = false Map the created databases to the corresponding TOML configuration sections: Database TOML Configuration WSO2IDENTITY_DB [database.identity_db] WSO2SHARED_DB [database.shared_db] WSO2AGENTIDENTITY_DB [datasource.AgentIdentity] WSO2DPDP_DB [datasource.WSO2DPDP_DB] For custom datasources ([datasource.AgentIdentity] and [datasource.WSO2DPDP_DB]), configure them using the following format: [datasource.WSO2DPDP_DB] id = "WSO2DPDP_DB" url = "jdbc:mysql://<database-host>:3306/WSO2DPDP_DB?autoReconnect=true&useSSL=false" username = "<database-user>" password = "<database-password>" driver = "com.mysql.cj.jdbc.Driver" pool_options.maxActive = "150" pool_options.maxWait = "60000" pool_options.minIdle = "5" pool_options.testOnBorrow = true pool_options.validationQuery = "SELECT 1" pool_options.validationInterval = "30000" pool_options.defaultAutoCommit = false Open the <IS_HOME>/repository/conf/deployment.toml file and update the datasource configurations: India's Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 (DPDP Act) establishes a framework for processing digital personal data that recognises both an individual's right to protect personal data and the need to process it for lawful purposes. The WSO2 DPDP Accelerator extends WSO2 Identity Server with consent, complaint (grievance), audit, and event-notification capabilities that help an organization put parts of that framework into operation. Disclaimer: This page is a product introduction, not legal advice or a statement of compliance. An organization remains responsible for determining how the Act, its commencement notifications, and applicable rules affect its processing activities.
documents.s: Digital Personal Data Protection and the WSO2 DPDP Accelerator

documents.t: The DPDP Act applies to digital personal data processed in India, including data collected in non-digital form and digitised later. It also applies to processing outside India when that processing is connected with offering goods or services to Data Principals (the individuals the personal data relates to) in India. The Act excludes specified personal or domestic processing and certain personal data made publicly available by the Data Principal or by a person legally required to publish it. The framework is built around several practical ideas: Process personal data for a lawful purpose, using consent or another use permitted by the Act. Give a clear notice and obtain consent that is free, specific, informed, unconditional, unambiguous, and expressed through clear affirmative action when consent is the basis for processing. Make withdrawing consent as easy as giving it and communicate the resulting change to the processors acting for the Data Fiduciary, the organization or person deciding why and how the data is processed. Keep personal data accurate where it is used to make decisions or disclosed to another Data Fiduciary, apply reasonable security safeguards, and respond to personal-data breaches. Provide ways for Data Principals to exercise their rights and raise grievances. The Act gives Data Principals rights to obtain specified information about processing, seek correction, completion, updating, or erasure, use grievance redressal, and nominate another individual to exercise their rights in the event of death or incapacity. It also places duties on Data Principals, such as not impersonating another person or submitting a false or frivolous grievance. The precise conditions and exceptions in the Act still apply to every right and obligation. The Act's provisions commence in phases. Use the official commencement notification to check when a provision takes effect; this product guide does not define a compliance deadline.

The diagram shows consent communicated through a Consent Manager, breach notification to the Board, and a complaint after exhausting grievance redressal. These relationships are described in sections 6, 8, and 13 of the Act. They describe the wider ecosystem; the accelerator does not submit complaints or breach notifications to the Board automatically. Participant Role under the Act Data Principal The individual to whom the personal data relates. The definition includes a parent or lawful guardian acting for a child, and a lawful guardian acting for a person with disability. Data Fiduciary Determines the purpose and means of processing, alone or with others, and remains responsible for processing performed on its behalf. Data Processor Processes personal data on behalf of a Data Fiduciary. A Data Fiduciary may engage a processor under a valid contract. Consent Manager A person registered with the Data Protection Board of India that provides an accessible, transparent, and interoperable platform through which a Data Principal can give, manage, review, and withdraw consent. Significant Data Fiduciary A Data Fiduciary notified by the Central Government based on factors in the Act and subject to additional obligations. Data Protection Board of India The statutory body established under the Act to perform the functions assigned to it, including handling personal-data-breach intimations and complaints. The accelerator helps a Data Fiduciary provide consent-management experiences. Installing it does not register the organization or the product as a statutory Consent Manager.

Priya Sharma uses CarePulse, an online healthcare app, to book an urgent virtual consultation with a specialist, order prescribed medications, and decide whether she wants her health trends analyzed for wellness perks. Data Principal - Priya Sharma (Patient)​ Reviews segregated notices: Reads distinct requests for medical consultation, prescription home delivery, and optional predictive health tips. Gives granular consent: Approves processing for her consult and prescription delivery, while explicitly ticking an opt-in box for weekly health insights. Exercises control: Later opens her privacy settings to withdraw permission for marketing and health trend profiling. Raises issues: Files a complaint via the portal when she mistakenly receives an unrequested promotional SMS after revoking consent. Data Fiduciary - CarePulse Telehealth (The Healthcare Platform)​ Defines purposes and data needs: Determines why data is required (e.g., vitals for consultation vs. address for courier delivery). Captures & audits consent: Employs the WSO2 DPDP Accelerator to record Priya's affirmative choices and record consent status and snapshot audit history. Coordinates the ecosystem: Communicates relevant consent changes to downstream consumers. Maintains accountability: Ensures legal basis compliance and oversees internal grievance resolution. Data Processor - MedExpress (Courier Partner) & CloudEngage (Marketing Vendor)​ Executes under contract: Processes Priya's delivery address (MedExpress) or email/phone (CloudEngage) strictly under CarePulse's instructions. Consumes lifecycle events: CloudEngage responds to consent changes and updates its active campaign pipeline. Grievance Officer / DPO - CarePulse Compliance Desk (Internal Team)​ Investigates concerns: Receives Priya's grievance ticket regarding the rogue SMS via the DPDP grievance portal. Reviews audit history: Checks the consent timeline and confirms that CloudEngage had a delivery lag when processing the revocation event. Resolves & intimates: Closes the gap with the vendor, updates the ticket, and delivers an official resolution within mandated statutory timelines. Data Protection Board of India (DPBI) - Statutory Regulatory Body​ Serves as final arbiter: Available as an escalation authority if Priya finds CarePulse's grievance response unsatisfactory or unfulfilled. Enforces accountability: Evaluates systemic non-compliance or data breaches reported by either Principals or the Fiduciary.

WSO2 Identity Server provides the identity, authentication, authorization, and core consent foundation, including APIs for purposes, data elements, and consent records. See Identity Server consent management. The WSO2 DPDP Accelerator extends that foundation with DPDP-focused consent management, audit, grievance handling, and lifecycle event capabilities that help organizations operationalize DPDP compliance.
documents.s: WSO2 Identity Server and the WSO2 DPDP Accelerator

documents.t: The accelerator runs with WSO2 Identity Server and provides a tenant-aware Consent Portal plus supporting services. Operational need Accelerator capability Define why data is requested Administrators maintain a reusable list of purposes and data elements, called the catalog, to describe what data is requested and why. Capture and manage consent Data Principals can view and manage their own consents, while authorized administrators can manage tenant-wide consent records. Demonstrate consent history Status audit and snapshot history preserve the recorded evolution of a consent for authorized review. Provide a grievance channel Data Principals can submit and track complaints; DPO and administrator views support assignment, messages, attachments, status changes, and due-date tracking. Propagate lifecycle changes Event Notification records consent and user lifecycle events and supports webhook or polling subscriptions for downstream consumers. Separate responsibilities Tenant roles distinguish personal history and complaint self-service, complaint handling, and broader portal administration. Dedicated integration roles can be created with narrower scopes. Support accessible notices The portal interface supports English and the languages listed in the Eighth Schedule to the Constitution; purpose and data-element descriptions can be localized separately. Support account lifecycle actions An authorized user can request self-service account deletion, and a lifecycle event can notify configured receivers. The accelerator also publishes lifecycle events for configured downstream systems, which can receive them through webhook or polling subscriptions.
