Even with consent management systems in place, issues can arise, such as unreflected consent withdrawals or concerns about personal data use. Data Principals need a clear way to raise grievances and track their resolution. The WSO2 DPDP Accelerator provides a grievance handling system that connects Data Principals with the organization's Data Protection Officer (DPO) to submit, investigate, and resolve complaints while maintaining an audit trail.

We'll continue using CarePulse, the online healthcare service introduced in the Understanding Consent guide. Priya is a Data Principal whose personal data is processed by CarePulse. She uses the Consent Portal to manage her consent and raise complaints when she has concerns. Ravi is CarePulse's Data Protection Officer (DPO). He reviews complaints, investigates issues, communicates with complainants, and coordinates the actions needed to resolve them.
documents.s: Meet the people in this example

documents.t: Priya previously withdrew her consent for optional marketing communications through the Consent Portal. CarePulse recorded the withdrawal and notified its external email provider, CloudEngage, so that her marketing preferences could be updated. However, CloudEngage received the notification but failed to update Priya's preferences. A few days later, she receives another marketing email. She raises a concern: I already opted out of marketing emails, but I'm still receiving them. Let's follow how CarePulse can investigate and handle her complaint.

Priya signs in to the Consent Portal and opens My Complaints. She then: Selects + Submit a complaint. Chooses Consent withdrawal issue and describes what happened. Attaches a screenshot of the unwanted email as supporting evidence. Submits the complaint. Priya's view (Data Principal): submitting a complaint. The portal creates a complaint record with a reference ID, such as CMP-2026-00001, allowing Priya and Ravi to identify and track the case. It also carries a statutory due date — the deadline by which CarePulse must resolve it under the DPDP Act — so Ravi can prioritize complaints that are close to breaching it. Priya can return to My Complaints to follow its progress and view updates. Try it: Submit a complaint.

Ravi opens Administration → Complaints and reviews Priya's complaint. To understand what happened, he examines the relevant consent history and works with the appropriate technical team to investigate how the marketing preferences are updated in CloudEngage. The investigation reveals that: Consent history: Priya's consent withdrawal was recorded successfully by CarePulse. Marketing preferences: CloudEngage received the notification but did not update Priya's marketing preferences. Ravi's view (DPO): reviewing Priya's complaint. These findings help Ravi establish that Priya's withdrawal was recorded correctly, but the external email provider continued using outdated preferences. With the cause identified, Ravi can coordinate the corrective actions needed to prevent further unwanted marketing emails.

Resolving a complaint often involves technical investigation, but the person who raised it still needs clear updates. The accelerator distinguishes between messages shared with the complainant and internal investigation notes. Public messages Ravi sends Priya an update through the complaint record: Hello Priya, we have confirmed that your consent was withdrawn successfully. We found that our email provider did not update your marketing preferences as expected. We are working with the provider to correct this. Priya can view this message in her complaint timeline. Internal notes Ravi can also record investigation details for authorized officers, such as: CloudEngage received the consent withdrawal notification but did not update the contact's marketing preferences. Coordinate with the vendor operations team to correct the preferences and verify that the contact is removed from active marketing campaigns. These notes help document technical findings and follow-up actions without exposing internal investigation details to the complainant. Ravi's view (DPO): public replies and internal notes together on the same complaint. Try it: Investigate and communicate.

Once CloudEngage confirms that Priya's marketing preferences have been corrected, Ravi updates the complaint's status to RESOLVED and records an explanation of the outcome. Priya can review the response and the complaint's recorded activity through the Consent Portal. Priya's view (Data Principal): the resolved complaint, with only the public replies visible. The complaint history provides a record of the investigation, communications, supporting evidence, and status changes. This helps CarePulse understand how the issue was handled and supports internal reviews and compliance activities. Try it: Resolve the complaint.

A complaint moves through a defined set of statuses as it progresses from submission to resolution. Status Meaning OPEN The complaint has been submitted and is awaiting review. IN_PROGRESS The DPO is investigating the complaint. WAITING_ON_CLIENT The DPO needs additional information from the complainant before continuing. AWAITING_INTERNAL_REVIEW The complainant has responded, and the DPO needs to review the response before proceeding. RESOLVED The complaint has been resolved. The complainant can reopen it if the issue continues.

Complaints follow defined status transitions rather than allowing arbitrary changes. A complaint can only move to the statuses listed for its current status: From Can move to OPEN IN_PROGRESS, WAITING_ON_CLIENT IN_PROGRESS WAITING_ON_CLIENT, RESOLVED WAITING_ON_CLIENT AWAITING_INTERNAL_REVIEW AWAITING_INTERNAL_REVIEW IN_PROGRESS, WAITING_ON_CLIENT, RESOLVED RESOLVED AWAITING_INTERNAL_REVIEW For example, a complaint cannot move directly from OPEN to RESOLVED; the DPO must pick it up first. Only the complainant can reopen a resolved complaint. For example, if Priya continues receiving marketing emails after her complaint is resolved, she sends a new message on the complaint in My Complaints. This moves it back to AWAITING_INTERNAL_REVIEW, so Ravi can review the new information and decide the next steps.

The accelerator separates complaint access according to each user's role. Data Principals manage their own complaints, while the DPO handles complaints across the organization. Role Responsibility and access dpdp-consent-user Can submit, view, and respond to their own complaints through the self-service portal, subject to the granted permissions. dpdp-consent-dpo Can review and manage tenant-wide complaints, send public replies, add internal notes, and update complaint statuses, subject to the granted permissions. The roles also use different API scopes and endpoint paths. Data Principals access their own complaints through self-service endpoints, while the DPO uses tenant-wide complaint management endpoints. For details about roles, permissions, and API access, see Managing Access.

Hands-on Walkthrough: Follow the step-by-step Try Out guide in Try Out: Complaints. Keep connected systems informed: See Event Notifications to learn how systems like CloudEngage find out about changes such as a consent withdrawal.

Consent is not just about asking for a yes or no. It involves understanding what personal data is needed, why it is needed, and giving people control over how their data is used. In practice, consent can change over time. People may give consent, update their preferences, or withdraw it altogether. Each of these decisions needs to be handled consistently throughout the consent lifecycle. This guide uses a simple example to explain how consent works in the DPDP Accelerator, from defining data requirements and collecting consent to managing changes, handling withdrawals, and understanding who can manage each consent.

Throughout this guide, we'll use CarePulse, an online healthcare service, to explain how consent works in practice. Priya is the Data Principal. She uses CarePulse and decides whether to give, change, or withdraw consent for the use of her personal data. CarePulse is the Data Fiduciary. It determines why Priya's personal data needs to be processed. Anika is CarePulse's Administrator. She manages the catalog of Purposes and Elements and oversees consent records within CarePulse's tenant. Raj is Priya's spouse. He appears later as the other person involved whenever a consent needs someone besides Priya to also decide.
documents.s: Meet the people in this example

documents.t: Before CarePulse asks Priya for consent, it needs to define what personal data it wants to use and for what purpose. This helps Priya understand what she is agreeing to. Anika sets this up in the catalog by defining the data elements and the purposes they support. For example: Define the data element. In Elements, Anika creates an element named contact-email, with a display name and description that explain what the data represents. Define the purpose. In Purposes, she creates a purpose named marketing-email, with version 1.0, and associates the contact-email element with it. Use the definition in a consent request. CarePulse can now use this configuration to explain the purpose and the data involved when asking Priya for consent. The key distinction is that Elements and Purposes define what data is needed and why, but they do not record anyone's consent. Creating an Element or Purpose alone does not mean Priya has agreed to anything. The connected application or the Consent Management API uses these definitions to create an actual consent record when Priya's consent is collected. Try it: Define a purpose and its data element.

Once CarePulse has defined its purposes and data requirements, its application can present the relevant consent choices to Priya. The application can use the Consent Management REST API to retrieve the available Purposes and their associated Elements, present them to Priya, and submit her decisions to create consent records. This allows applications to integrate consent collection into their own user journeys. For example, while creating her account, Priya is asked whether she wants to receive marketing emails. She agrees, and CarePulse submits her choice through the Consent Management API to create a consent record for the marketing-email purpose, covering the contact-email element defined earlier.

A consent record captures the purposes Priya agreed to and the specific data elements covered by each purpose. It does not automatically include every element associated with a purpose. For example, suppose CarePulse later adds an optional phone-number element to the marketing-email purpose, so it can also send promotional text messages. If Priya agrees to marketing emails but declines to share her phone number, the consent request includes only the contact-email element: { ... "purposes": [ { "id": "<marketing-email-purpose-id>", "elements": [ { "id": "<contact-email-element-id>" } ] } ] ... } If Priya also agrees to share her phone number, CarePulse includes the phone number element ID in the same elements array. The consent record also captures the version of the purpose used when the consent was created. This helps establish which version of the purpose the consent refers to. To manage consents using the REST API, see the API calls in Try Out: Consent.
documents.s: Record the purposes and data elements selected

documents.t: After giving consent, Priya can open My Consents in the Consent Portal to review her consent records, including what she agreed to, which service requested the consent, its current status, and when it expires. Anika, as CarePulse's Administrator, can use All Consents to review tenant-wide consent records, subject to her permissions. The Consent Portal allows individuals and administrators to review and manage consent records according to their roles. Try it: Review, authorize, revoke, and audit a consent.
documents.s: Review consent in the Consent Portal

documents.t: Consent can change over time. A person may update their choices or decide to withdraw consent they previously gave. For example, several weeks after agreeing to marketing emails, Priya decides she no longer wants to receive them. She opens My Consents in the Consent Portal, finds her marketing-email consent, and withdraws it. The Consent Management API records the change, allowing the consent history to show: What changed When the change occurred Which purpose version was involved How the consent progressed through its lifecycle

Withdrawing consent updates the consent record, but it does not automatically delete personal data already held by CarePulse or its Data Processors. CarePulse must handle the consequences of the withdrawal according to applicable requirements, including stopping processing that relies on the withdrawn consent where required. Any necessary follow-up actions, such as notifying Data Processors or handling data under applicable retention requirements, depend on the relevant obligations and system integrations. The Event Notifications feature can help CarePulse communicate consent changes to connected systems so they can take the appropriate action. See Event Notifications for more information. Try it: Review, authorize, revoke, and audit a consent.
documents.s: What happens after consent is withdrawn?

documents.t: A consent moves through a defined lifecycle. Its current state indicates whether it is awaiting a decision, in effect, or has been rejected, revoked, or expired. State Meaning PENDING The consent is awaiting a decision from one or more required authorizers. ACTIVE The consent has received all required approvals and is in effect. REJECTED A required authorizer rejected the consent. REVOKED The consent was withdrawn. An active consent can be revoked by the subject of a direct consent or by an authorizer, and an administrator can revoke a consent that is pending or active. EXPIRED The consent has reached its expiry time.

The initial state depends on how the consent is configured: No authorizers specified: The consent becomes ACTIVE immediately. One or more authorizers specified: The consent starts as PENDING and becomes ACTIVE only after all required authorizers approve it. An authorizer rejects a pending consent: The consent becomes REJECTED.
documents.s: How does a consent become active?

documents.t: The accelerator supports three consent models based on who is involved in authorizing a consent: direct, delegated, and co-authorized consent.

In direct consent, the subject gives consent for themself. No additional authorizers are required. This is the model behind Priya's marketing-email consent from earlier in this guide: { "subjectId": "priya@example.com", "purposes": [ { "id": "<marketing-email-purpose-id>", "elements": [ { "id": "<contact-email-element-id>" } ] } ] } Because no additional authorizers are specified, the consent becomes ACTIVE immediately. Priya can manage her own consent, including revoking it after it becomes active. Try it: Review, authorize, revoke, and audit a consent.

In delegated consent, one or more people authorize the use of data on behalf of the subject. This model is useful when a parent gives consent for a child or a guardian acts on behalf of a dependent. For example, both parents may be required to approve a consent for their child: { "subjectId": "child@example.com", "purposes": [ { "id": "<purpose-id>", "elements": [ { "id": "<element-id>" } ] } ], "authorizations": [ { "userId": "mother@example.com", "type": "USER" }, { "userId": "father@example.com", "type": "USER" } ] } The consent remains PENDING until both parents approve it. If either parent rejects it, the consent becomes REJECTED. In this model, the subject is an observer only. They can view the consent but cannot approve, reject, revoke, or otherwise manage it. Once the consent is active, any of the named authorizers can revoke it, and an administrator can revoke it while it is pending or active. The same mechanism applies whenever someone other than the subject must authorize on their behalf — for example, CarePulse naming Raj as the sole authorizer on a consent for Priya's enrollment in a shared family health plan. Try it: Authorize consent as a guardian or delegate.

Co-authorized consent is useful when the subject must participate in the authorization decision alongside one or more other people. For example, Priya and Raj are joint subscribers to a shared CarePulse family plan. CarePulse requires both account holders to approve a consent covering data shared between their accounts, including Priya herself as the subject: { "subjectId": "priya@example.com", "purposes": [ { "id": "<purpose-id>", "elements": [ { "id": "<element-id>" } ] } ], "authorizations": [ { "userId": "priya@example.com", "type": "USER" }, { "userId": "raj@example.com", "type": "USER" } ] } Because both Priya and Raj are authorizers, the consent remains PENDING until both approve it. If either rejects it, the consent becomes REJECTED. Unlike delegated consent, the subject in a co-authorized consent is an active participant in the decision and can approve or reject the consent as an authorizer. Try it: Create a co-authorized consent.

Creating a consent record does not automatically ensure that an application uses personal data in accordance with that consent. Before processing personal data, the consuming application should verify that the consent is valid for the intended operation. The application can retrieve the full consent record using the Consent Management REST API: curl "${BASE_URL}/api/identity/consent-mgt/v2.0/consents/<consent-id>" \ -H "Authorization: Bearer ${ACCESS_TOKEN}" To try it, use a consent ID and the CarePulse application's token from Try Out: Consent. The response provides information about the consent, including its current state, the purposes it covers, and the associated data elements. For example, a consent response might include: { "id": "<consent-id>", "state": "ACTIVE", "purposes": [ { "name": "marketing-email", "version": "1.0", "elements": [ { "id": "<element-id>", "name": "contact-email", "displayName": "Contact email" } ] } ] } Before processing the data, the consuming application should check that: The consent is active. Its current state permits the intended processing. The purpose matches. The intended processing is covered by a purpose included in the consent. The required data elements are covered. The consent includes the specific data elements the application intends to use. These checks help ensure that the application respects the person's recorded choices and does not rely on an earlier approval without verifying the consent's current state and scope.
documents.s: Review and enforce consent before processing

When a person withdraws consent or their personal data changes, other systems that hold or process that data may need to know about the change so they can take the appropriate action. Event Notifications enables the WSO2 DPDP Accelerator to communicate these changes to connected systems automatically, without relying on manual notifications. For example, when Priya (Data Principal) withdraws consent for marketing communications, CarePulse (Data Fiduciary) records the change and notifies CloudEngage (Data Processor), its email service provider. CloudEngage can then update Priya's marketing preferences to reflect her decision. This guide explains how Event Notifications works, how to configure subscriptions, and how to ensure that events are delivered securely and reliably.

We'll continue using CarePulse, the online healthcare service introduced in the Understanding Consent guide. Priya is a Data Principal who uses CarePulse and whose personal data is processed by the service. CarePulse is the Data Fiduciary. It determines why Priya's personal data is processed. CloudEngage is a Data Processor that sends marketing emails on CarePulse's behalf. MedExpress is a Data Processor that delivers orders for CarePulse. Anika is CarePulse's Administrator. She configures and manages Event Notifications through the Consent Portal.
documents.s: Meet the people in this example

documents.t: Event Notifications connects changes in the DPDP Accelerator with the systems that need to know about them. The process follows three main steps: An event is produced. A relevant change occurs, such as Priya (Data Principal) withdrawing consent, or a connected application publishes a custom event. The event is matched to subscribers. Event Notifications identifies the subscriptions configured to receive events on the relevant topic and applies any configured filters. The event is delivered. The subscriber receives the event through a webhook or retrieves it through polling, depending on its subscription configuration. The receiving system then processes the event and takes the appropriate action. The diagram above illustrates the consent lifecycle, event production, subscription matching, and event delivery, including the alternative paths for publishing custom events and retrieving events through polling.

Event Notifications uses four core concepts to connect changes with the systems that need to know about them. Topic: A category of change that subscribers can listen for, such as consent.revoke. The accelerator provides standard topics for consent and account changes, and CarePulse (Data Fiduciary) can define custom topics for its own events. Subscription: A Data Processor's registration to receive events for one or more topics. A subscription specifies how events should be delivered, either through a webhook endpoint or by allowing the processor to retrieve events through polling. It can also include filters, such as consent-purpose restrictions. Event: A record of a specific change, such as Priya (Data Principal) withdrawing consent for marketing communications. An event is associated with a topic and can be made available to systems subscribed to that topic. Delivery: The process of making an event available to a particular subscriber. Each subscriber's delivery is tracked separately, allowing delivery outcomes to be monitored independently when an event is sent to multiple subscribers. Understanding these concepts makes it easier to follow how events are produced, matched to subscriptions, and delivered.

Events can originate from different parts of the system. Consent lifecycle events: WSO2 Identity Server generates events when relevant consent or account changes occur. For example, when Priya (Data Principal) withdraws consent, the accelerator can publish a consent.revoke event. Custom events: A connected application, such as CarePulse (Data Fiduciary), can publish events to custom topics through the Event Notifications API. These events can represent business-specific changes, such as updates to delivery preferences. This allows the accelerator to communicate changes arising from its own lifecycle operations while also supporting events originating from connected applications.

Before events can be delivered, the Data Fiduciary's administrator configures subscriptions for the Data Processors that need to receive notifications. For example, CarePulse (Data Fiduciary) may need CloudEngage (Data Processor) to receive consent revocation events related to marketing communications, while MedExpress (Data Processor) may need to retrieve delivery preference updates. To configure a webhook subscription, the administrator follows these steps: Collect webhook details. Obtain the Data Processor's webhook URL and any other required configuration details. Configure the subscription. Through the Consent Portal, select the event topics the Data Processor needs to receive, such as consent.revoke, and configure the webhook endpoint. Share the secret. Securely share the required subscription secret with the Data Processor so it can verify the subscription signature associated with incoming notifications. For example, CarePulse collects CloudEngage's webhook URL. Anika (Data Fiduciary Administrator) creates a subscription for consent.revoke events and securely shares the required secret with CloudEngage. Anika's view (Data Fiduciary Administrator): registering a webhook subscription for consent revocation events. The Data Fiduciary is responsible for ensuring that its Data Processors are appropriately configured and have the necessary contractual obligations to act on relevant notifications. The administrator manages the technical setup, including subscriptions, webhook settings, and credentials.

The accelerator supports two delivery methods. Each subscription uses one of them. Webhooks: Event Notifications pushes events to an endpoint that the Data Processor hosts. For example, CloudEngage (Data Processor) can receive a consent.revoke event and update Priya (Data Principal)'s marketing preferences. To receive webhook notifications, the Data Processor must run its own webhook listener: a service on its side that accepts requests from the accelerator. The requests the accelerator sends to this listener, and the responses it expects back, are defined in webhook-listener.openapi.yaml. You can use the sample listeners in Node.js and Python as starting points. Polling: The Data Processor periodically calls the accelerator to fetch available events, so it doesn't need to host a listener. For example, MedExpress (Data Processor) can retrieve relevant updates when polling for events. A successful delivery confirms receipt, not completion. Data Processors can also report when they've finished handling an event through event completion reporting, which we'll cover later in this guide.

Suppose Priya (Data Principal) withdraws her consent for marketing communications. Priya withdraws consent. She withdraws her consent through the Consent Portal, and CarePulse (Data Fiduciary) records her decision. The accelerator publishes an event. WSO2 Identity Server generates the relevant consent lifecycle event, and the accelerator publishes a consent.revoke event. Event Notifications identifies the subscribers. The system determines which subscriptions are configured to receive the event's topic and applies any relevant filters. The event is delivered. CloudEngage (Data Processor) receives the event through its configured webhook or retrieves it through polling. CloudEngage updates its records. It processes the notification and updates Priya's marketing preferences so that the withdrawn consent is respected. This approach helps CarePulse keep connected systems informed of important changes without requiring manual notification for every event.

The accelerator automatically publishes events on five built-in topics covering the consent and account lifecycle. Topic Published when consent.update A consent's state changes, such as an approval or rejection. consent.revoke A consent is revoked. consent.expire A consent passes its expiry time. user.data.change A user's profile data is modified. user.account.delete A user account is deleted. Subscribe Data Processors to the topics relevant to their responsibilities. For example, CloudEngage (Data Processor) may need consent.revoke events to maintain marketing preferences, while another processor may need to respond to account deletion events.

Not every Data Processor needs to receive every consent-related event. Purpose-based filtering helps limit notifications to the events relevant to a processor's responsibilities. For example, Anika (Data Fiduciary Administrator) configures CloudEngage (Data Processor)'s subscription to receive consent revocation events associated with the marketing-email purpose. This allows CloudEngage to receive relevant notifications without receiving events for unrelated consent purposes. Subscriptions can be configured for all purposes, specific purposes, or all purposes except selected ones. Account events are not associated with consent purposes, so purpose-based filtering does not apply to them. Try it: Subscribe to consent revocation events
documents.s: Delivering events to relevant Data Processors

documents.t: Not all events originate from consent lifecycle operations. Connected applications can also publish custom events to communicate business-specific changes. Consider MedExpress (Data Processor), which runs behind a firewall that blocks incoming webhook calls. Its subscription uses polling instead, allowing MedExpress to retrieve events without requiring the accelerator to initiate connections to its endpoint. When a customer updates their delivery preferences, CarePulse (Data Fiduciary)'s order system publishes a custom event on a topic that Anika (Data Fiduciary Administrator) created: delivery.preferences.update. MedExpress periodically requests available events from the accelerator, processes the events it receives, and acknowledges each one so that it is not delivered again. Custom events follow the same subscription and delivery process as built-in events. The main difference is that a connected application publishes them to a custom topic rather than relying on a built-in lifecycle event. Try it: Publish your own event and poll for it
documents.s: Publishing custom events and retrieving them through polling

documents.t: Before acting on a notification about Priya (Data Principal)'s consent, CloudEngage (Data Processor) needs to verify that the event is genuine and that the signed content has not been tampered with. The accelerator supports two layers of signature verification. Event signature: WSO2 Identity Server signs the JWT event payload using its private key. CloudEngage can verify this signature using the corresponding public key published through the Identity Server's JWKS endpoint. This helps verify the event payload's authenticity and integrity. Subscription signature: Each delivery includes a signature generated using the shared subscription secret. CloudEngage verifies this signature to check the delivery against the configured subscription. These signatures serve different purposes: the event signature verifies the signed event payload, while the subscription signature verifies the delivery's association with the subscriber's subscription. Signatures do not encrypt event contents. Use HTTPS to protect notifications in transit, and avoid including unnecessary personal data in event payloads. Where possible, use references such as a consent ID rather than including personal data directly. Try it: Understand what the shared secret protects

Webhook endpoints may become temporarily unavailable because of network issues, maintenance, or other failures. Event Notifications provides delivery tracking and retry mechanisms to help administrators identify and investigate these problems. Suppose CloudEngage (Data Processor)'s server is unavailable when Priya (Data Principal) withdraws her consent. The delivery fails. The accelerator cannot successfully deliver the event to CloudEngage's webhook endpoint. The accelerator retries. Event Notifications retries the delivery according to the configured retry policy. The delivery is marked Failed if retries are exhausted. If the delivery continues to fail, Anika (Data Fiduciary Administrator) can inspect the event and its delivery history under Event Notifications → Events. The administrator investigates. After addressing the underlying issue, Anika can retry the delivery when appropriate. Anika's view (Data Fiduciary Administrator): a delivery that exhausted all its retry attempts, now marked Failed with a Retry option. A subscription can also be marked Stale if its webhook endpoint fails the verification check used to confirm that it is ready to receive events. This indicates a subscription or endpoint readiness issue that may need investigation. Try it: Confirm that the processor was notified For more details, see Inspect events and delivery history.
documents.s: Handling failed deliveries and unavailable endpoints

documents.t: Receiving a notification doesn't necessarily mean that the required action has been taken. A Data Processor still needs to process the event and act on the change. To help track this, the DPDP Accelerator supports event completion reporting. This allows a Data Processor to report when it has successfully handled an event, recording that confirmation alongside the delivery. For example, when Priya (Data Principal) withdraws her marketing consent, CloudEngage (Data Processor) receives a notification and updates her marketing preferences. For webhook deliveries, there are two important things to understand: Delivered: CloudEngage's server confirms that it received the notification by returning a successful 2xx HTTP response. This doesn't mean CloudEngage has finished processing the event. Anika's view (Data Fiduciary Administrator): the event detail page, with the delivery to CloudEngage (Data Processor)'s subscription shown as Delivered. Completion evidence: After updating Priya's marketing preferences, CloudEngage can submit a signed completion report. This doesn't change the delivery's status away from Delivered — instead, the completion is recorded alongside it as evidence that the required action was carried out. Anika's view (Data Fiduciary Administrator): the same delivery after CloudEngage (Data Processor) submits its completion report, now showing Completion Evidence alongside the Delivered status. Completion can only be reported once a delivery has already reached Delivered, and only once per delivery. The completion report must also be signed using the subscription's shared secret so the accelerator can verify that it came from CloudEngage. For details on how to submit a completion report, see Submit webhook delivery completion in the Event Notification Guide, or the POST /deliveries/{deliveryId}/completion operation in the DPDP Event Notification API specification. In short: Delivered means the notification was received. Completion evidence means the Data Processor has additionally reported that it successfully handled the event. By combining subscriptions, event delivery, signature verification, and delivery tracking, the DPDP Accelerator helps organizations communicate important changes to connected systems and monitor the outcome of those notifications.

This guide helps you understand the WSO2 DPDP Accelerator through practical examples and common use cases. Each section focuses on a specific need and shows how the accelerator supports it. The sections are connected, so you can see how different capabilities work together. note The examples in this guide are intended to help you understand how the accelerator can be used. You can adapt the configuration and workflows to suit your organization's requirements.

Once you have set up the DPDP Accelerator, you can start exploring it using the following URLs. Component URL Identity Server Console https://<HOST>/console Consent Portal https://<HOST>/consent-portal/ These are the main starting points for exploring the DPDP Accelerator. You can use the sections in this guide to understand what you can do with these components and how the different capabilities work together. Using a tenant? The URLs above are for the super tenant. If you're working within a specific tenant, insert /t/<tenant-domain> before the path, for example https://<HOST>/t/<tenant-domain>/console. See WSO2's multi-tenancy guide for more on how tenants work.
Learn how access is managed for portal users, administrators, and API integrations.
Learn how users can give, review, and revoke consent, and how these actions are managed by the accelerator.
Learn how a Data Principal can raise a complaint and how an organization can manage and respond to it.
Learn how connected systems are notified when important changes occur, such as consent being updated or revoked, or user data changing.

Managing Access — roles, permissions, and direct API access. Consent — the consent lifecycle, from defining a purpose to withdrawing consent. Complaint — how grievances are raised, tracked, and resolved. Event Notifications — how connected systems stay informed of important changes.

The DPDP Accelerator provides two ways to access its capabilities: Access to the Consent Portal — control what users can do when they sign in to the Consent Portal. Direct API access — allow applications and backend systems to call the accelerator APIs directly using an access token. If you are setting up access for people who use the Consent Portal, start with Part 1: Managing access to the Consent Portal. If you are integrating the accelerator with another application or testing its APIs using curl or Postman, go to Part 2: Managing access to the APIs directly.

The DPDP Accelerator includes the Consent Portal, which is used by different types of users. Since the same portal is used for different purposes, each user is assigned a role that determines what they can access and manage.
documents.s: Part 1: Managing access to the Consent Portal

documents.t: The DPDP Accelerator comes with three predefined roles. Each role includes a set of permissions that defines what the user can do in the Consent Portal. Role Intended for What they can do dpdp-consent-user Data Principal Manage their own consents, view history and track their own complaints etc. dpdp-consent-admin Data Fiduciary Administrator Manage all consents, purposes and data elements and manage event notifications dpdp-consent-dpo Data Protection Officer and complaint-handling staff View and manage complaints across the organization.

Roles provide a convenient way to group permissions, while scopes are what the system actually checks when a user performs an action. For example, the Data Fiduciary Administrator role has a broader set of scopes because administrators need access to more functionality. The Data Principal role has only the scopes required for users to manage their own data and complaints. You can also create custom roles when the built-in roles do not match your organization's requirements. Assign only the scopes required for each role. tip Haven't created your users yet? Follow Configuring Users and Roles to create users and assign these roles before continuing.

The following sections provide the technical mapping between API operations, required scopes, and the built-in roles. You normally do not need to work with these scope names when assigning the predefined roles. They are mainly useful when you are creating custom roles, configuring an API integration, or troubleshooting an authorization error.

Operation Required scope(s) Admin Data principal DPO Sign in and manage own consents internal_login ✓ ✓ ✓ View or manage other users' consents internal_consent_mgt_consent_view, internal_consent_mgt_consent_create, internal_consent_mgt_consent_update ✓ ✗ ✗ View purposes internal_consent_mgt_purpose_view ✓ ✗ ✗ Create, update, or delete purposes internal_consent_mgt_purpose_create, internal_consent_mgt_purpose_update, internal_consent_mgt_purpose_delete ✓ ✗ ✗ View data elements internal_consent_mgt_element_view ✓ ✗ ✗ Create or delete data elements internal_consent_mgt_element_create, internal_consent_mgt_element_delete ✓ ✗ ✗

Operation Required scope Admin Data principal DPO View own status-audit history consent:status-history:view:self ✓ ✓ ✗ View own full snapshot history consent:history:view:self ✓ ✓ ✗ View organization-wide status-audit history consent:status-history:view:any ✓ ✗ ✗ View organization-wide full snapshot history consent:history:view:any ✓ ✗ ✗

Operation Required scope(s) Admin Data principal DPO Create, view, reply to, or transition own complaints complaints:read:self, complaints:write:self ✗ ✓ ✗ View or manage any complaint in the organization complaints:read:any, complaints:write:any ✗ ✗ ✓

Operation Required scope Admin Data principal DPO View topics notifications:topics:read ✓ ✗ ✗ Create or deregister topics notifications:topics:write ✓ ✗ ✗ View subscriptions and delivery history notifications:subscriptions:read ✓ ✗ ✗ Create, verify, or delete subscriptions notifications:subscriptions:write ✓ ✗ ✗ View events and delivery history notifications:events:read ✓ ✗ ✗ Publish events notifications:events:write ✓ ✗ ✗ Poll event deliveries notifications:events:poll ✓ ✗ ✗ Submit delivery-completion evidence notifications:event-deliveries:complete ✓ ✗ ✗ The last two scopes are for systems that receive events. The dpdp-consent-admin role holds them, but the Consent Portal doesn't request them when an administrator signs in, so a portal token never carries them. Give each publishing or receiving system its own application with only the scopes it needs, for example: Integration Scopes to assign event-publisher notifications:events:write event-receiver notifications:events:poll, notifications:event-deliveries:complete

The roles described above control access for users of the Consent Portal. For system-to-system integrations, you can use a machine-to-machine application to access the accelerator APIs. This is useful for testing APIs with curl or Postman, integrating the accelerator with another system, or running backend services that call the APIs.
documents.s: Part 2: Managing access to the APIs directly

documents.t: Sign in to the Identity Server Console: https://<HOST>/console Select Applications from the left navigation. Click New Application. Select Machine-to-Machine Application. This application type is intended for backend services and scripts that need to access APIs without an interactive user login. Enter a name for the application, such as my-integration, and click Create. Open the Protocol tab and note the Client ID and Client Secret. You will use these credentials to obtain an access token. Keep the client secret secure. Do not commit it to source control or expose it in client-side applications.

After creating the application, authorize the scopes required by the APIs you want to call. Open the application's API Authorization tab. Click Authorize an API. Select the API you want to access, such as DPDP Consent History, Complaints, or Event Notification. Select the scopes required by your integration. Only authorize the permissions the application actually needs. For example, an application that only publishes events should not be given complaint-management or consent-management permissions. Refer to the scope tables above to identify the scopes required for each operation. Each scope belongs to one API resource in the Console: API resource Scopes Consent Management V2 – Consents, Purposes, and Elements internal_consent_mgt_* DPDP Consent History consent:status-history:view:self, consent:status-history:view:any, consent:history:view:self, consent:history:view:any DPDP Complaint Management API complaints:read:self, complaints:write:self, complaints:read:any, complaints:write:any DPDP Event Notification API topics notifications:topics:read, notifications:topics:write DPDP Event Notification API subscriptions notifications:subscriptions:read, notifications:subscriptions:write DPDP Event Notification API events notifications:events:read, notifications:events:write DPDP Event Notification API poll notifications:events:poll DPDP Event Notification API deliveries notifications:event-deliveries:complete

Use the client ID and client secret of your machine-to-machine application to request an access token using the OAuth 2.0 client_credentials grant. curl -X POST "https://<HOST>/oauth2/token" \ -H "Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded" \ -d "grant_type=client_credentials" \ -d "client_id=<CLIENT_ID>" \ -d "client_secret=<CLIENT_SECRET>" \ -d "scope=internal_consent_mgt_consent_view" Replace the following placeholders with values from your environment: <HOST> — the hostname of your Identity Server <CLIENT_ID> — the client ID of your machine-to-machine application <CLIENT_SECRET> — the client secret of your machine-to-machine application Replace internal_consent_mgt_consent_view with the scopes authorized for your application. For multiple scopes, separate them with spaces. Local testing with a self-signed certificate Add -k to the curl command above if your local Identity Server uses the default self-signed certificate. Never use -k in production — configure a trusted CA certificate, or pass it explicitly with --cacert instead.

Once you have the access token, include it as a Bearer token in the API request. For example, fetching all consents in the tenant: curl "https://<HOST>/api/identity/consent-mgt/v2.0/consents" \ -H "Authorization: Bearer <ACCESS_TOKEN>" Replace <ACCESS_TOKEN> with the access_token value from the response in Step 3. The API validates the access token and checks whether it contains the scope required for the requested operation.

If the request fails, check the HTTP status code: 401 Unauthorized — The access token is missing, invalid, or expired. Obtain a new access token and try again. 403 Forbidden — The access token is valid, but it does not contain the scope required by the API. Return to Step 2 and authorize the required scope for the application. A token keeps the scopes it was issued with. After you change an application's authorized scopes or a user's roles, obtain a new token.

Try Out: Consent — see the scopes and tokens from this page used in a real API call. Consent — learn how consent is given, reviewed, and revoked. Configuring Users and Roles — create users and assign the built-in roles.

Keep a copy of every file you edit and reapply it afterwards.

Use this for fixing a typo or improving the wording of the portal's built-in labels, buttons, and messages — not for anything related to a specific Purpose or Element (see section 3 for that). Open <IS_HOME>/repository/deployment/server/webapps/consent-portal/i18n/<lang-code>/common.json for the language you're correcting. Find the key and edit its value. Keep the key name and JSON structure exactly as they are — only change the text between the quotes. Save. No restart needed. Adding a brand-new piece of UI text (one that doesn't exist in any language yet) is not an operator task — it requires a code change and a rebuild of the accelerator, since something has to be built to display it. Raise that with the engineering team.
documents.s: 2. Correcting the portal's own UI text (common.json)

documents.t: Purposes and Elements are created at run time by administrators through the portal, so their wording isn't part of the accelerator build — each language's catalog.json starts out empty and is filled in as items get translated: { "purposes": {}, "elements": {} } Purposes can only have their description translated; Elements can have both displayName and description. To add a translation for an Element or Purpose: Open catalog.json for the target language. Add an entry keyed by the item's exact name — displayName and/or description under elements, description only under purposes: { "purposes": { "marketing_via_email@1.0": { "description": "ईमेल के माध्यम से मार्केटिंग" } }, "elements": { "email-address": { "displayName": "ईमेल पता", "description": "उपयोगकर्ता का ईमेल पता" } } } The key must match the item's name exactly, character for character. For a Purpose whose wording differs between versions, key that version specifically as name@version, using the version exactly as it was entered when the Purpose was created (for example "marketing_via_email@2.0"), instead of just name. If a Purpose has no version-specific entry, its plain name entry (if any) applies to every version. Elements are never versioned, so this only applies under purposes. Save. No restart needed. Until a language has an entry for a given item, readers in that language see the wording the administrator entered when creating it, not an error or a blank field. You don't need to translate every item before going live.

Not currently supported as a configuration change — the set of languages offered by the switcher is built into the accelerator. Adding one requires an engineering change and a rebuild; raise it with the engineering team rather than attempting it by adding a new i18n/<lang-code>/ folder on a running deployment.

The WSO2 DPDP Accelerator helps you build solutions for India's Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023. Built on top of WSO2 Identity Server,Solution provides consent management, grievance handling, consent audit history, and event notifications, along with a Consent Portal for end users and administrators. This guide sets up the accelerator in a local environment with the default embedded H2 databases, so you can quickly try it out. Setting up for production? This quickstart is for local evaluation only. For a production deployment, follow Install and Set Up instead.

Java Development Kit: JDK 21. Environment variables: set JAVA_HOME to the JDK 21 folder and add its bin folder to your PATH. Linux macOS Windows export JAVA_HOME="<JDK_LOCATION>" export PATH=$JAVA_HOME/bin:$PATH java -version export JAVA_HOME="$(/usr/libexec/java_home -v 21)" export PATH=$JAVA_HOME/bin:$PATH java -version $env:JAVA_HOME = "<JDK_LOCATION>" $env:Path = "$env:JAVA_HOME\bin;$env:Path" java -version java -version should report version 21.
Download WSO2 Identity Server 7.3.0 and extract the ZIP.

Download the latest wso2-dpdpiam-accelerator-<version>.zip from the releases page. To build it from source instead, see the repository README. Extract it, and copy the extracted wso2-dpdpiam-accelerator-<version> directory into the root directory of Identity Server. The rest of this guide refers to the directories as follows: Directory Placeholder Identity Server <IS_HOME> DPDP Accelerator, inside <IS_HOME> <DPDP_ACCELERATOR_HOME>

The accelerator needs Identity Server at U2 update level 17 or later. A freshly downloaded Identity Server doesn't include the update tool yet, so get it first: Go to <IS_HOME>/bin and run the setup script. It downloads the update tool that matches your operating system and processor into the same folder: Linux macOS Windows ./update_tool_setup.sh ./update_tool_setup.sh .\update_tool_setup.ps1 Then, in the same folder, run the update tool it downloaded: Linux macOS Windows ./wso2update_linux # ARM64: ./wso2update_linux_arm64 ./wso2update_darwin_arm64 # Intel: ./wso2update_darwin .\wso2update_windows.exe # ARM64: .\wso2update_windows_arm64.exe If the tool reports that it updated itself, run the same command again to update Identity Server. For more information about WSO2 updates and the update tool, see updating WSO2 products.

Go to <IS_HOME>/<DPDP_ACCELERATOR_HOME>/bin and run the merge script, then the configure script: Linux macOS Windows ./merge.sh ./configure.sh ./merge.sh ./configure.sh The accelerator's scripts are Bash scripts, so run them from Git Bash or WSL (Windows Subsystem for Linux): ./merge.sh ./configure.sh

Go to <IS_HOME>/bin and start Identity Server: Linux macOS Windows ./wso2server.sh ./wso2server.sh .\wso2server.bat Once the server starts, open the Console at https://localhost:9443/console and sign in with the default administrator account: username admin@wso2.com, password wso2123.

To fully try out the accelerator, create users and assign them these roles by following the Configuring Users and Roles User Role What they can do in the portal Portal administrator dpdp-consent-admin Manage purposes and elements, view and revoke any user's consents, view consent history, and manage Event Notifications. Complaints are handled by the Data Protection Officer. Use this user to check the portal in the next step. Data Principal dpdp-consent-user Exercise their data protection rights: review the history of their consents, raise and track grievances, and delete their own account. Data Protection Officer dpdp-consent-dpo View and respond to every complaint in the organization, without access to consents or other administration.
Open https://localhost:9443/consent-portal/ and sign in as the user holding dpdp-consent-admin.

Explore how the WSO2 DPDP Accelerator supports complaint management, from submission by a Data Principal to investigation and resolution by a Data Protection Officer (DPO). The example continues the CarePulse (Data Fiduciary) story: Priya raises a complaint, and Ravi handles it. For the complete list of endpoints and schemas, see the Complaint Server API specification.

Ensure WSO2 Identity Server with the DPDP Accelerator is installed and running. Create these users and assign their roles, as described in Configuring Users and Roles: Priya (Data Principal), username priya@example.com: dpdp-consent-user Ravi (Data Protection Officer), username ravi@example.com: dpdp-consent-dpo Create one application for CarePulse and authorize it for the DPDP Complaint Management API, with the complaints:read:any and complaints:write:any scopes. This guide primarily uses the Consent Portal. REST API examples are also provided for the officer's operations. Before running the API examples, set the base URL and access token. Obtain a client-credentials token using the CarePulse application's credentials, with the complaints:read:any and complaints:write:any scopes. export BASE_URL="https://localhost:9443" export ACCESS_TOKEN="<carepulse-client-credentials-token>" The base URL is for the super tenant. For a specific tenant, use https://localhost:9443/t/<tenant-domain>. Local testing with a self-signed certificate Add -k to the curl commands if your local Identity Server uses the default self-signed certificate. Never use -k in production — configure a trusted CA certificate, or pass it with --cacert.

Sign in to the Consent Portal as Priya and open Complaints → My Complaints. Select + Submit a complaint and enter the details: Category: for example, Consent withdrawal issue. Description: explain the issue without including unnecessary sensitive personal data. For example: "I revoked my consent for marketing purposes, but I am still receiving promotional messages." Attachments (optional): upload one file as supporting evidence, such as a screenshot. Supported formats are PNG, JPG, PDF, and DOCX, up to 10 MB. You can add more evidence later in follow-up messages, one file per message. Select Submit complaint. Confirm that the complaint appears in My Complaints with a reference ID (for example, CMP-2026-00001), status, and submission date. Open the complaint to review its status and statutory due date. The Activity tab shows the timeline and supports public follow-up messages; the Attachments tab lists the submitted evidence. An application can also submit a complaint on Priya's behalf, using her own user token, through POST /api/dpdp/complaints/v1/me/complaints. See the Complaint Server API specification for the request format.
documents.s: Step 1: Submit a complaint as Priya (Data Principal)

documents.t: Sign in as Ravi and open Administration → Complaints. Find the complaint by its reference ID and open it. Review the complaint details, due date, and evidence in the Attachments tab. Use Reply to send a message visible to Priya, such as "We are reviewing your request." Use Internal note for investigation notes that only officers can see. Sign back in as Priya and verify that the public reply appears in the activity timeline and the internal note is not visible.

Use the CarePulse application's client-credentials token for officer-level requests. The token must include the complaints:read:any and complaints:write:any scopes. Replace <complaint-id> with the complaint's ID. Retrieve the complaint details, including Priya's description and any associated attachments: curl \ "${BASE_URL}/api/dpdp/complaints/v1/complaints/<complaint-id>" \ -H "Authorization: Bearer ${ACCESS_TOKEN}" Post a public reply and move the complaint to IN_PROGRESS in one request: curl -X POST \ "${BASE_URL}/api/dpdp/complaints/v1/complaints/<complaint-id>/comments" \ -H "Authorization: Bearer ${ACCESS_TOKEN}" \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{ "message": "We are reviewing your request.", "isPublic": true, "toStatus": "IN_PROGRESS" }' To add an internal note instead, set "isPublic": false. Internal notes are visible to officers only.

As Ravi, open the complaint and use the status menu beside the comment composer. Select Resolved, enter a final message describing the outcome, and submit it. Confirm that the complaint shows Resolved. Sign back in as Priya and verify that the resolution message and status appear in My Complaints. To resolve the complaint through the API, send the same comments request with "toStatus": "RESOLVED" and a message describing the outcome. A message is required when resolving.
