Explore the consent lifecycle using CarePulse (Data Fiduciary): define what data is needed, create a consent, review and revoke it as the Data Principal, and inspect the audit record. The scenario also covers consents that another person must authorize.

Ensure WSO2 Identity Server with the DPDP Accelerator is installed and running. Create these users and assign their roles, as described in Configuring Users and Roles: Priya (Data Principal), username priya@example.com: dpdp-consent-user Raj (additional authorizer), username raj@example.com: dpdp-consent-user Anika (Data Fiduciary Administrator): dpdp-consent-admin Create one application for CarePulse and authorize it for the Consent Management V2 – Consents and DPDP Consent History APIs. Before running the API examples, set the base URL and access token. Obtain a client-credentials token using the CarePulse application's credentials, with the scopes required for the operations below. export BASE_URL="https://localhost:9443" export ACCESS_TOKEN="<carepulse-client-credentials-token>" The base URL is for the super tenant. For a specific tenant, use https://localhost:9443/t/<tenant-domain>. Local testing with a self-signed certificate Add -k to the curl commands if your local Identity Server uses the default self-signed certificate. Never use -k in production — configure a trusted CA certificate, or pass it with --cacert.
CarePulse first defines which data it needs (an element) and why (a purpose).
documents.s: Define a purpose and its data element

documents.t: Sign in to the Consent Portal as Anika. Open Elements and select Add element. Enter: Field Value Name contact-email Display name Contact email Description Email address used to send optional product updates. Select Create, then open the new row and note its ID.

Open Purposes and select Add purpose. Enter: Field Value Name marketing-email Type optional-marketing Version 1.0 Description Send occasional product news by email. Add the contact-email element and leave it optional. Select Create, then open the purpose and note its ID. Expected result: both appear in the catalog, ready for CarePulse to use when it creates a consent.
CarePulse records Priya's consent for marketing emails. Priya reviews it and later withdraws it, and Anika checks the audit record.
documents.s: Review, authorize, revoke, and audit a consent

documents.t: The portal can't create consents, so CarePulse creates it through the API, using the access token you set earlier (how to get a token). The token needs the internal_consent_mgt_consent_create scope. For the full request format, see the Consent Management v2 API reference. Replace the two IDs with the ones you noted. curl -X POST "${BASE_URL}/api/identity/consent-mgt/v2.0/consents" \ -H "Authorization: Bearer ${ACCESS_TOKEN}" \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{ "subjectId": "priya@example.com", "serviceId": "CarePulse-client", "purposes": [ { "id": "<marketing-email-purpose-id>", "elements": [ { "id": "<contact-email-element-id>" } ] } ], "language": "en", "expiryTime": 1990411096000, "authorizations": [], "properties": {} }' There are no other authorizers, so this is a Direct Consent and it's ACTIVE straight away. Note the returned consent ID.
Sign in to the Consent Portal as Priya. Open My Consents and select the new consent. Check its purpose and data element. The authorizations table is empty, because no one else needs to approve it.
documents.s: Step 2: Review the consent as Priya (Data Principal)

documents.t: On the same page, select Revoke and confirm. Reopen it and check that its state is REVOKED, with the change shown in Consent Lifecycle.
documents.s: Step 3: Revoke the consent as Priya

documents.t: Sign in as Anika and open Administration → All Consents. Find Priya's consent (filter by consent ID, user, or state) and open it. Anika sees every consent in the organization. Priya only sees her own.
documents.s: Step 4: Inspect the consent as Anika (Data Fiduciary Administrator)

documents.t: You can use the DPDP Consent History API to verify the consent's lifecycle history independently of the portal. Use the CarePulse application's client-credentials token. To read the history, the token must include the consent:status-history:view:any scope, as defined in the Consent History API contract. curl "${BASE_URL}/api/dpdp/consent-mgt/v1/consents/<consent-id>/status-history?limit=100&offset=0" \ -H "Authorization: Bearer ${ACCESS_TOKEN}" Representative response after revocation (the IDs and timestamps will differ in your environment): { "consentId": "81c6dcb8-3df9-4b15-a43e-50f253792dbe", "statusHistory": [ { "previousStatus": "ACTIVE", "currentStatus": "REVOKED", "actionType": "REVOKE", "actionBy": "priya@example.com", "actionTime": 1788230520000 } ], "pagination": { "limit": 100, "offset": 0, "totalCount": 1 } } Expected result: the consent is REVOKED, and the status history records the transition from ACTIVE to REVOKED.

A Delegated Consent allows someone other than the Data Principal to make the authorization decision. The Data Principal can view the consent, but the designated authorizer is responsible for authorizing it. In this example, CarePulse creates a consent for Priya and designates Raj as the additional authorizer. The API records the Data Principal and the required authorizers but does not verify whether an authorizer is a parent, legal guardian, or other authorized representative. The Data Fiduciary must verify this relationship before creating the delegated consent.
documents.s: Authorize consent as a guardian or delegate

documents.t: Ensure that Priya and Raj have separate test accounts. Create the consent with the same CarePulse application's client-credentials token, using the purpose and element IDs from Define a purpose and its data element. The access token must include the internal_consent_mgt_consent_create scope. For details, see the Consent Management v2 API reference. curl -X POST \ "${BASE_URL}/api/identity/consent-mgt/v2.0/consents" \ -H "Authorization: Bearer ${ACCESS_TOKEN}" \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{ "subjectId": "priya@example.com", "serviceId": "CarePulse-client", "purposes": [ { "id": "<marketing-email-purpose-id>", "elements": [ { "id": "<contact-email-element-id>" } ] } ], "language": "en", "expiryTime": 1990411096000, "authorizations": [ { "userId": "raj@example.com", "type": "USER" } ], "properties": {} }' subjectId already identifies the person whose data the consent concerns, while authorizations contains the additional people who must decide on that person's behalf. When at least one authorization is supplied, Identity Server stores the new consent as PENDING.

Sign in to the Consent Portal as Priya and open My Pending Consents. Open the consent. Since Priya is not a named authorizer, the page explains that it is waiting for authorization instead of showing Approve/Reject actions.
documents.s: Step 2: Observe the consent as Priya

documents.t: Sign in to the Consent Portal as Raj, the authorizer. Open the consent from My Consents, filtered to Managed, or open My Pending Consents. Confirm the Data Principal, service, purpose, data elements, and authorization entry. Raj sees Approve/Reject actions that Priya does not. Select Approve and confirm. Reopen the consent and confirm that Raj's authorization is APPROVED. Because Raj is the only required authorizer in this example, the aggregate consent becomes ACTIVE. If several authorizers were supplied, it would remain PENDING until all required authorizers approved.
documents.s: Step 3: Approve the consent as Raj, the delegate

documents.t: Sign back in to the Consent Portal as Priya. Open My Consents and choose Personal. Open the consent and verify that it is ACTIVE and records Raj's approved authorization. Inspect Consent Lifecycle and View Full Snapshot History to confirm that the authorization and aggregate state transition were audited.
documents.s: Step 4: Verify the result as Priya

documents.t: Unlike delegated consent, a Co-authorized Consent names the Data Principal as one of the authorizers alongside at least one other person. In this example, both Priya and Raj must approve the same consent.

Use the CarePulse application's client-credentials token and the purpose and element IDs from Define a purpose and its data element. Include both Priya and Raj in the authorizations list. The access token must include the internal_consent_mgt_consent_create scope. For details, see the Consent Management v2 API reference. curl -X POST \ "${BASE_URL}/api/identity/consent-mgt/v2.0/consents" \ -H "Authorization: Bearer ${ACCESS_TOKEN}" \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{ "subjectId": "priya@example.com", "serviceId": "CarePulse-client", "purposes": [ { "id": "<marketing-email-purpose-id>", "elements": [ { "id": "<contact-email-element-id>" } ] } ], "language": "en", "expiryTime": 1990411096000, "authorizations": [ { "userId": "priya@example.com", "type": "USER" }, { "userId": "raj@example.com", "type": "USER" } ], "properties": {} }'

Sign in as Priya and open My Consents, filtered to Managed. Approve Priya's own authorization entry. Reopen the consent and confirm that Priya's decision is recorded. The overall consent remains PENDING until Raj also makes his decision.
Sign in as Raj and open the same consent from My Consents, filtered to Managed, or from My Pending Consents. Review the consent and approve Raj's own authorization entry.

Reopen the consent as Priya or Raj. With both authorizations APPROVED, the aggregate consent becomes ACTIVE. Both named authorizers are required to approve independently before it becomes active. This differs from the other models: Direct Consent: no named authorizers; the consent becomes ACTIVE immediately. Delegated Consent: the subject is not a named authorizer; another person makes the authorization decision. Co-authorized Consent: the subject and at least one other person are named authorizers and must each make a decision.

Learn: Understanding Consent: the concepts behind these flows. Try Out: Complaint Management: submit and resolve a complaint. Try Out: Event Notifications: notify connected systems when a consent changes.

Event Notifications tell connected systems when something changes, such as a consent being revoked or a user account being deleted. Subscribers receive each event at a webhook listener or by polling for it. This guide continues the CarePulse (Data Fiduciary) story and walks you through two flows: Notify a processor when a consent is revoked: subscribe a webhook listener, revoke a consent, verify the delivery, and report that the processor acted on it. Publish your own event and poll for it: register a custom topic, publish an event through the REST API, and retrieve and acknowledge it by polling. They use three building blocks: Topic: the kind of change you want to hear about, such as consent.revoke. The accelerator ships system topics for consent and user lifecycle changes. Subscription: a processor signing up for a topic. Each event reaches the processor either at its webhook listener or when it polls for it. Event and delivery history: a record of every event published and every attempt to deliver it, which you can look through in the Consent Portal. Here are the system topics and what triggers each one: System topic Triggered when consent.update A consent is updated, or an authorizer approves or rejects it consent.revoke A consent is revoked consent.expire The expiry reconciler records a consent as expired user.data.change A user's profile claims are updated user.account.delete A user account is deleted For the complete list of endpoints and schemas, see the Event Notification API specification.

Ensure WSO2 Identity Server with the DPDP Accelerator is installed and running. Create these users and assign their roles, as described in Configuring Users and Roles: Priya (Data Principal), username priya@example.com: dpdp-consent-user Anika (Data Fiduciary Administrator): dpdp-consent-admin Create an application for each system below and authorize it for the listed APIs and scopes: Application Role in this guide APIs and scopes CarePulse Data Fiduciary: creates the test consent and publishes the custom event Consent Management V2 – Consents (internal_consent_mgt_consent_create), DPDP Event Notification API subscriptions (notifications:subscriptions:write), DPDP Event Notification API events (notifications:events:write) CloudEngage Data Processor: reports completion of a webhook delivery DPDP Event Notification API deliveries (notifications:event-deliveries:complete) MedExpress Data Processor: polls for and acknowledges events DPDP Event Notification API poll (notifications:events:poll) Giving each application only the scopes it needs keeps the publisher and the receivers separate. Before running the API examples, set the base URL, the group ID, and the CarePulse application's access token. Obtain a client-credentials token using the CarePulse application's credentials, with the scopes listed above. Each step that needs the CloudEngage or MedExpress token says so. Linux macOS Windows export BASE_URL="https://localhost:9443" export API_BASE="${BASE_URL}/api/dpdp/event-notifications/v1" export GROUP_ID="carbon.super" export ACCESS_TOKEN="<carepulse-client-credentials-token>" export BASE_URL="https://localhost:9443" export API_BASE="${BASE_URL}/api/dpdp/event-notifications/v1" export GROUP_ID="carbon.super" export ACCESS_TOKEN="<carepulse-client-credentials-token>" $env:BASE_URL = "https://localhost:9443" $env:API_BASE = "$env:BASE_URL/api/dpdp/event-notifications/v1" $env:GROUP_ID = "carbon.super" $env:ACCESS_TOKEN = "<carepulse-client-credentials-token>" These values are for the super tenant. For a specific tenant, use https://localhost:9443/t/<tenant-domain> as the base URL and the tenant domain as the group ID, and get every token from that same tenant. Local testing with a self-signed certificate Add -k to the curl commands if your local Identity Server uses the default self-signed certificate. On Windows, add -SkipCertificateCheck to Invoke-RestMethod; this needs PowerShell 7 or later, so with Windows PowerShell 5.1, trust the server's certificate instead. Never skip certificate checks in production — configure a trusted CA certificate, or pass it with --cacert.

When a Data Principal revokes their consent, every Data Processor holding their data has to stop using it. In this flow: Priya (Data Principal) revokes a consent in My Consents. Anika (Data Fiduciary Administrator) registers the subscription under Event Notifications → Subscriptions and checks the delivery under Events. CloudEngage (Data Processor) receives the consent.revoke event at its webhook listener, which runs outside the portal.
documents.s: Notify a processor when a consent is revoked

documents.t: A webhook listener receives the subscription verification and each event delivery from Identity Server. Its API contract is in webhook-listener.openapi.yaml. For this try-out, use one of the sample listeners below. Each sample listener is a single file, with nothing to install. It answers the verification challenge, checks every delivery's signature with the shared secret, and prints whatever it receives. Node.js (webhook-listener.mjs) needs Node.js 18 or later: Linux macOS Windows node --version curl -O https://raw.githubusercontent.com/wso2/dpdp-accelerator/main/docs/static/examples/webhook-listener.mjs export SHARED_SECRET="carepulse-sample-secret-9d3e7b12" node webhook-listener.mjs node --version curl -O https://raw.githubusercontent.com/wso2/dpdp-accelerator/main/docs/static/examples/webhook-listener.mjs export SHARED_SECRET="carepulse-sample-secret-9d3e7b12" node webhook-listener.mjs node --version curl.exe -O https://raw.githubusercontent.com/wso2/dpdp-accelerator/main/docs/static/examples/webhook-listener.mjs $env:SHARED_SECRET = "carepulse-sample-secret-9d3e7b12" node webhook-listener.mjs Python (webhook-listener.py) needs Python 3.9 or later: Linux macOS Windows python3 --version curl -O https://raw.githubusercontent.com/wso2/dpdp-accelerator/main/docs/static/examples/webhook-listener.py export SHARED_SECRET="carepulse-sample-secret-9d3e7b12" python3 webhook-listener.py python3 --version curl -O https://raw.githubusercontent.com/wso2/dpdp-accelerator/main/docs/static/examples/webhook-listener.py export SHARED_SECRET="carepulse-sample-secret-9d3e7b12" python3 webhook-listener.py python --version curl.exe -O https://raw.githubusercontent.com/wso2/dpdp-accelerator/main/docs/static/examples/webhook-listener.py $env:SHARED_SECRET = "carepulse-sample-secret-9d3e7b12" python webhook-listener.py Once it's running, the listener prints its local address and confirms that HMAC signature checks are enabled: ============================================================= DPDP Reference Webhook Listener (Node.js) Listening on: http://127.0.0.1:8443/dpdp/events HMAC Verification: ENABLED (shared secret configured) Press Ctrl+C to stop. ============================================================= The address shown in the terminal is local to your machine. Identity Server must be able to reach the listener, so the subscription needs a callback URL it can reach. For local testing, see Exposing a listener locally below. Make sure to use a strong shared secret in a production environment. Understand the two signature checks Event contents are signed, not encrypted. HTTPS protects the contents in transit. Two separate signatures have different purposes: Event JWT signature: Identity Server signs the event JWT with its tenant private key. A receiver should verify the JWT signature using the matching public key published through Identity Server's JWKS endpoint. This verifies the event's authenticity and integrity. Delivery HMAC (event-signature): webhook deliveries also carry an HMAC of the request body, calculated with the subscription's shared secret. The sample listener checks this HMAC, so someone who finds your callback URL can't send it fake events. The shared secret is also used for the signed event's payloadHash, and to sign poll requests and completion reports. These checks don't encrypt event data or replace validating the event JWT signature. Avoid putting unnecessary personal data in payloads; use references, such as a consent ID, wherever possible. Exposing a listener locally No public server to run the listener on? Try one of these: An ngrok tunnel. Set up ngrok, run ngrok http 8443 in a second terminal, then add /dpdp/events to the https:// forwarding address it prints. That's your callback URL for Step 3. Your test events travel through ngrok, so stick to sample data, and don't use a tunnel for a real receiver. Your machine's network IP, if Identity Server can't reach the internet. Start the listener with HOST set to that IP, and use http://<ip>:8443/dpdp/events as the callback URL. Identity Server turns away private network addresses by default, so also set allow_private_network_callback_targets = true under [dpdp_accelerator.event_notifications.webhook] in deployment.toml and restart it. If you've set allow_http_callback_url = false in the same section, set it back to true for this test, because the callback uses HTTP. Keep allow_private_network_callback_targets set to false in production.

The portal can't create consents, so CarePulse creates one through the API, and Priya revokes it in the portal in Step 4. Get a purpose ID and an element ID. Sign in to the Consent Portal as Anika, go to Definitions → Purposes, and open the marketing-email purpose. No purpose yet? Create one with an element first, as described in Define a purpose and its data element. Copy the Purpose ID from the purpose page, then open one of its elements and copy its ID as well. Create an active consent for Priya with the CarePulse token you set earlier. The token needs the internal_consent_mgt_consent_create scope. subjectId must belong to a user in the same tenant. On the highlighted line, swap in the <purpose-id> and <element-id> you copied: Linux macOS Windows curl -X POST "${BASE_URL}/api/identity/consent-mgt/v2.0/consents" \ -H "Authorization: Bearer ${ACCESS_TOKEN}" \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{ "subjectId": "priya@example.com", "serviceId": "CarePulse-client", "language": "en", "purposes": [ { "id": "<purpose-id>", "elements": [ { "id": "<element-id>" } ] } ] }' curl -X POST "${BASE_URL}/api/identity/consent-mgt/v2.0/consents" \ -H "Authorization: Bearer ${ACCESS_TOKEN}" \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{ "subjectId": "priya@example.com", "serviceId": "CarePulse-client", "language": "en", "purposes": [ { "id": "<purpose-id>", "elements": [ { "id": "<element-id>" } ] } ] }' $Body = @' { "subjectId": "priya@example.com", "serviceId": "CarePulse-client", "language": "en", "purposes": [ { "id": "<purpose-id>", "elements": [ { "id": "<element-id>" } ] } ] } '@ Invoke-RestMethod -Method Post ` -Uri "$env:BASE_URL/api/identity/consent-mgt/v2.0/consents" ` -Headers @{ Authorization = "Bearer $env:ACCESS_TOKEN" } ` -ContentType "application/json" ` -Body $Body | ConvertTo-Json -Depth 10 There are no other authorizers, so the consent is ACTIVE straight away. The response includes its id; use your own ID rather than the example IDs shown later.
documents.s: Step 2: Create a consent to revoke

documents.t: Sign in to the Consent Portal as Anika. Open Event Notifications → Subscriptions and select Register Subscription. Enter a Subscription Name, such as CloudEngage - consent revocations. Set Topic Category to Consent Topics, and select consent.revoke under Topics. Set Consent Purpose Filter Mode to Specific Purposes, and select marketing-email under Consent Purposes. The listener then hears only about revocations of consents that include this purpose. To hear about every revocation, choose All Purposes instead. Set Delivery Mode to Webhook, enter your callback URL from Step 1 as the Webhook Callback URL (for example, https://<your-ngrok-address>/dpdp/events), and enter carepulse-sample-secret-9d3e7b12 as the Shared Secret. Select Register Subscription. Right away, Identity Server sends the listener a verification challenge. As soon as the listener answers it, the subscription turns Active: Over in the listener's terminal, you'll see the challenge it answered: [INFO] ================ [SUBSCRIPTION VERIFICATION] ================ [INFO] Verification Payload: { "type": "subscription.verification", "subscriptionId": "e4e10144-e76a-4d4b-9e80-70747df4f650", "topics": [ "consent.revoke" ], "challenge": "ec09e7a8-fb5b-4eec-9670-c3c1fbe529b9" } [INFO] Verified subscription 'e4e10144-e76a-4d4b-9e80-70747df4f650' for topics: ["consent.revoke"] [INFO] <-- Returned HTTP 200 OK with challenge: 'ec09e7a8-fb5b-4eec-9670-c3c1fbe529b9' Using the REST API (optional)​ To register the subscription through the API instead, use the CarePulse token. It must include the notifications:subscriptions:write scope. Linux macOS Windows curl -X POST "${API_BASE}/subscriptions" \ -H "Authorization: Bearer ${ACCESS_TOKEN}" \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{ "name": "CloudEngage - consent revocations", "topics": ["consent.revoke"], "filter": { "type": "specific", "purposes": ["marketing-email"] }, "delivery": { "mode": "webhook", "callbackUrl": "https://<your-ngrok-address>/dpdp/events", "sharedSecret": "carepulse-sample-secret-9d3e7b12" } }' curl -X POST "${API_BASE}/subscriptions" \ -H "Authorization: Bearer ${ACCESS_TOKEN}" \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{ "name": "CloudEngage - consent revocations", "topics": ["consent.revoke"], "filter": { "type": "specific", "purposes": ["marketing-email"] }, "delivery": { "mode": "webhook", "callbackUrl": "https://<your-ngrok-address>/dpdp/events", "sharedSecret": "carepulse-sample-secret-9d3e7b12" } }' $Body = @' { "name": "CloudEngage - consent revocations", "topics": ["consent.revoke"], "filter": { "type": "specific", "purposes": ["marketing-email"] }, "delivery": { "mode": "webhook", "callbackUrl": "https://<your-ngrok-address>/dpdp/events", "sharedSecret": "carepulse-sample-secret-9d3e7b12" } } '@ Invoke-RestMethod -Method Post ` -Uri "$env:API_BASE/subscriptions" ` -Headers @{ Authorization = "Bearer $env:ACCESS_TOKEN" } ` -ContentType "application/json" ` -Body $Body | ConvertTo-Json -Depth 10 The subscription name must be unique in the tenant, so use a different name if you already registered one in the portal.
documents.s: Step 3: Subscribe the listener to consent revocations

documents.t: Sign in to the Consent Portal as Priya. Open My Consents and select the consent you created. It should show Active. Select Revoke, then Revoke Consent to confirm. The consent now shows Revoked. An application can also revoke a consent on Priya's behalf, using her own user token (not the CarePulse token), through POST /api/users/v1/me/consents/<consent-id>/revoke.

Within a few seconds, the event reaches the listener. The sample checks the delivery HMAC and prints the decoded event, including the consent ID Priya just revoked: [INFO] ==================== [EVENT DELIVERY] ==================== [INFO] Delivery-Id: 58328a80-4e74-44c8-80cc-927414e4159a [INFO] Event-Signature: sha256=e8c0443706bca2452875971e20bdc909867a12298bbd99907d36edcbf4092245 [INFO] HMAC-SHA256 signature verified successfully. [INFO] Decoded Event Payload: { "iss": "https://localhost:9443/oauth2/token", "sub": "carbon.super", "aud": "dpdp-event-notifications", ... "payload": { "deliveryId": "58328a80-4e74-44c8-80cc-927414e4159a", "eventId": "131b9ab4-c6f2-4652-ae70-023dafc35c8f", "subscriptionId": "e4e10144-e76a-4d4b-9e80-70747df4f650", "orgId": "carbon.super", "groupId": "carbon.super", "topic": "consent.revoke", "eventPayload": { "consentId": "c540bcee-c9d8-4919-8fdc-e2b9723971f5", "previousStatus": "ACTIVE" } } } [INFO] <-- Returned HTTP 202 Accepted You can find the same event in the portal too. As Anika, open Event Notifications → Events, and search for the eventId from the listener output, or look for the newest consent.revoke event: Open it to see the payload and the delivery to your subscription, marked Delivered: Notice that the event carries only the consent ID and its previous status, none of Priya's personal data. A real processor would use consentId to find the data it holds under that consent and stop using it. Expected result: revoking the consent publishes a consent.revoke event, and CloudEngage's listener receives it because the subscription matches both the topic and the marketing-email purpose. Delivered means the listener accepted the notification; CloudEngage is still responsible for acting on it. For more on this, see receiver responsibilities.
documents.s: Step 5: Confirm that the processor was notified

documents.t:
You can stop after Step 5 if you only want to verify webhook delivery. Continue here to see how a processor reports that it has acted on an event. A 2xx response from the listener confirms receipt, not completion. After CloudEngage has updated Priya's marketing preferences, it can submit a signed completion report, so the accelerator records that confirmation alongside the delivery. Obtain a client-credentials token using the CloudEngage application's credentials, with the notifications:event-deliveries:complete scope. Use the deliveryId from your Step 5 listener output, and the same shared secret you used for the subscription. The signature is an HMAC-SHA256, made with the shared secret, over v1, completion, the delivery ID, and the exact request body, each on its own line. This binds the report to one delivery. completionEvidence must be an HTTPS URL. Linux macOS Windows export CLOUDENGAGE_TOKEN="<cloudengage-access-token>" export SHARED_SECRET="carepulse-sample-secret-9d3e7b12" DELIVERY_ID="<delivery-id-from-step-5>" COMPLETION_BODY='{"completionStatus":"completed","completionEvidence":"https://cloudengage.example/evidence/receipt.pdf"}' COMPLETION_SIGNATURE="sha256=$(printf 'v1
completion
%s
%s' "${DELIVERY_ID}" "${COMPLETION_BODY}" \ | openssl dgst -sha256 -hmac "${SHARED_SECRET}" | awk '{print $NF}')" curl -X POST "${API_BASE}/deliveries/${DELIVERY_ID}/completion" \ -H "Authorization: Bearer ${CLOUDENGAGE_TOKEN}" \ -H "group-id: ${GROUP_ID}" \ -H "event-signature: ${COMPLETION_SIGNATURE}" \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d "${COMPLETION_BODY}" export CLOUDENGAGE_TOKEN="<cloudengage-access-token>" export SHARED_SECRET="carepulse-sample-secret-9d3e7b12" DELIVERY_ID="<delivery-id-from-step-5>" COMPLETION_BODY='{"completionStatus":"completed","completionEvidence":"https://cloudengage.example/evidence/receipt.pdf"}' COMPLETION_SIGNATURE="sha256=$(printf 'v1

%s' "${DELIVERY_ID}" "${COMPLETION_BODY}" \ | openssl dgst -sha256 -hmac "${SHARED_SECRET}" | awk '{print $NF}')" curl -X POST "${API_BASE}/deliveries/${DELIVERY_ID}/completion" \ -H "Authorization: Bearer ${CLOUDENGAGE_TOKEN}" \ -H "group-id: ${GROUP_ID}" \ -H "event-signature: ${COMPLETION_SIGNATURE}" \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d "${COMPLETION_BODY}" $env:CLOUDENGAGE_TOKEN = "<cloudengage-access-token>" $env:SHARED_SECRET = "carepulse-sample-secret-9d3e7b12" $DeliveryId = "<delivery-id-from-step-5>" $CompletionBody = '{"completionStatus":"completed","completionEvidence":"https://cloudengage.example/evidence/receipt.pdf"}' $Hmac = [System.Security.Cryptography.HMACSHA256]::new([Text.Encoding]::UTF8.GetBytes($env:SHARED_SECRET)) $SigningInput = "v1`ncompletion`n$DeliveryId`n$CompletionBody" $CompletionSignature = 'sha256=' + [BitConverter]::ToString($Hmac.ComputeHash([Text.Encoding]::UTF8.GetBytes($SigningInput))).Replace('-', '').ToLower() Invoke-RestMethod -Method Post ` -Uri "$env:API_BASE/deliveries/$DeliveryId/completion" ` -Headers @{ Authorization = "Bearer $env:CLOUDENGAGE_TOKEN" "group-id" = $env:GROUP_ID "event-signature" = $CompletionSignature } ` -ContentType "application/json" ` -Body $CompletionBody A successful call returns 204 No Content. Reopen the event in Event Notifications → Events: the delivery still shows Delivered, now with Completion Evidence recorded alongside it. Submitting a second completion for the same delivery returns 409 Conflict (EN-4090). For the other completion statuses and error responses, see Submit webhook delivery completion.

The accelerator publishes consent and user lifecycle events on its own. Your applications can publish events too, about their own business changes, on topics you define. Say CarePulse's order system publishes an event whenever a customer updates their delivery preferences. MedExpress, the delivery processor (Data Processor), sits behind a firewall and can't expose a webhook. Instead, it polls for new events and acknowledges each one once it has processed it. In this flow: Anika (Data Fiduciary Administrator) registers the custom topic and the poll subscription in the Consent Portal, and checks the result. CarePulse publishes the event through the REST API, using its own token. MedExpress polls for the event and acknowledges it through the REST API, using its own token. Obtain a client-credentials token using the MedExpress application's credentials, with the notifications:events:poll scope: Linux macOS Windows export MEDEXPRESS_TOKEN="<medexpress-access-token>" export MEDEXPRESS_TOKEN="<medexpress-access-token>" $env:MEDEXPRESS_TOKEN = "<medexpress-access-token>"
documents.s: Publish your own event and poll for it

documents.t: Sign in to the Consent Portal as Anika. Open Event Notifications → Topics and select Register Topic. Enter delivery.preferences.update as the Topic Name, add a Description, and select Register Topic.

Open Event Notifications → Subscriptions and select Register Subscription. Enter a Subscription Name, such as MedExpress - delivery preferences. Set Topic Category to Custom Topics, and select delivery.preferences.update under Topics. Keep Consent Purpose Filter Mode as All Purposes. Set Delivery Mode to Poll. Enter medexpress-sample-secret-4f8a2c91 as the Shared Secret. MedExpress signs its poll requests with it. We use a sample value so the commands below work as they are. For a real receiver, select the generate icon at the end of the field instead, and keep the secret somewhere safe. Select Register Subscription. Poll subscriptions don't need verification, so this one is Active straight away. Copy its Subscription ID with the copy icon in the list: Linux macOS Windows export SUBSCRIPTION_ID="<subscription-id>" export SHARED_SECRET="medexpress-sample-secret-4f8a2c91" export SUBSCRIPTION_ID="<subscription-id>" export SHARED_SECRET="medexpress-sample-secret-4f8a2c91" $env:SUBSCRIPTION_ID = "<subscription-id>" $env:SHARED_SECRET = "medexpress-sample-secret-4f8a2c91"

Now play CarePulse's order system and publish the change with the CarePulse token. It must include the notifications:events:write scope. The group-id header has to match the subscription's group, which is the tenant domain (carbon.super for the super tenant). An event with any other group ID is stored, but reaches no subscriber. Linux macOS Windows curl -X POST "${API_BASE}/events" \ -H "Authorization: Bearer ${ACCESS_TOKEN}" \ -H "group-id: ${GROUP_ID}" \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{ "topic": "delivery.preferences.update", "payload": { "customerReference": "cust-0001", "change": "DELIVERY_WINDOW_UPDATED" } }' curl -X POST "${API_BASE}/events" \ -H "Authorization: Bearer ${ACCESS_TOKEN}" \ -H "group-id: ${GROUP_ID}" \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{ "topic": "delivery.preferences.update", "payload": { "customerReference": "cust-0001", "change": "DELIVERY_WINDOW_UPDATED" } }' $Body = @' { "topic": "delivery.preferences.update", "payload": { "customerReference": "cust-0001", "change": "DELIVERY_WINDOW_UPDATED" } } '@ Invoke-RestMethod -Method Post -Uri "$env:API_BASE/events" ` -Headers @{ Authorization = "Bearer $env:ACCESS_TOKEN" "group-id" = $env:GROUP_ID } ` -ContentType "application/json" ` -Body $Body | ConvertTo-Json -Depth 10 You'll get back the stored event and its eventId: { "eventId": "f0b66a0d-edcb-4d94-94ee-70ce33b34f20", "orgId": "carbon.super", "groupId": "carbon.super", "topicId": "3064830b-7249-4fa6-9b83-59d7215af1c2", "payload": "{\"customerReference\":\"cust-0001\",\"change\":\"DELIVERY_WINDOW_UPDATED\"}", "occurredAt": 1791199075832, "createdAt": 1791199075832 } Try to keep personal data out of the payload. Send a reference the receiver can look up instead, the way customerReference does here.

Next, switch to MedExpress and poll with the MedExpress token. The first poll can have an empty body: Linux macOS Windows POLL_BODY='' POLL_SIGNATURE="sha256=$(printf %s "${POLL_BODY}" | openssl dgst -sha256 -hmac "${SHARED_SECRET}" | awk '{print $NF}')" curl -X POST "${API_BASE}/events/poll" \ -H "Authorization: Bearer ${MEDEXPRESS_TOKEN}" \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -H "group-id: ${GROUP_ID}" \ -H "subscription-id: ${SUBSCRIPTION_ID}" \ -H "event-signature: ${POLL_SIGNATURE}" \ -d "${POLL_BODY}" POLL_BODY='' POLL_SIGNATURE="sha256=$(printf %s "${POLL_BODY}" | openssl dgst -sha256 -hmac "${SHARED_SECRET}" | awk '{print $NF}')" curl -X POST "${API_BASE}/events/poll" \ -H "Authorization: Bearer ${MEDEXPRESS_TOKEN}" \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -H "group-id: ${GROUP_ID}" \ -H "subscription-id: ${SUBSCRIPTION_ID}" \ -H "event-signature: ${POLL_SIGNATURE}" \ -d "${POLL_BODY}" $PollBody = '' $Hmac = [System.Security.Cryptography.HMACSHA256]::new([Text.Encoding]::UTF8.GetBytes($env:SHARED_SECRET)) $PollSignature = 'sha256=' + [BitConverter]::ToString($Hmac.ComputeHash([Text.Encoding]::UTF8.GetBytes($PollBody))).Replace('-', '').ToLower() Invoke-RestMethod -Method Post -Uri "$env:API_BASE/events/poll" ` -Headers @{ Authorization = "Bearer $env:MEDEXPRESS_TOKEN" "group-id" = $env:GROUP_ID "subscription-id" = $env:SUBSCRIPTION_ID "event-signature" = $PollSignature } ` -ContentType "application/json" ` -Body $PollBody | ConvertTo-Json -Depth 10 event-signature is an HMAC-SHA256 of the exact request body, made with the subscription's shared secret. For an empty body, it's calculated over zero bytes. The server only checks it when request_hmac_validation_enabled = true under [dpdp_accelerator.event_notifications.polling], and that's off by default. Sign every request anyway, so your receiver keeps working when someone turns the check on. The response holds pending deliveries in the sets object. Each key is a delivery ID, and its value is a signed event (a compact JWS) carrying the same contents as a webhook delivery. Save the delivery ID, because you'll need it in Step 5 to acknowledge the event: { "moreAvailable": false, "sets": { "07f813ee-391a-4cd2-aa70-2ebe420fc0d0": "eyJhbGciOiJSUzI1NiIsInR5cCI6IkpXVCIs..." } } Before you trust an event, verify its signature against Identity Server's JWKS endpoint. Once it checks out, you'll find your event in the payload claim, under eventPayload: "eventPayload": { "change": "DELIVERY_WINDOW_UPDATED", "customerReference": "cust-0001" }

Once MedExpress has processed the event, it sends the delivery ID back in the next poll's ack array, signing the new body the same way: Linux macOS Windows DELIVERY_ID="<delivery-id-from-step-4>" POLL_BODY="{\"ack\": [\"${DELIVERY_ID}\"], \"maxEvents\": 20}" POLL_SIGNATURE="sha256=$(printf %s "${POLL_BODY}" | openssl dgst -sha256 -hmac "${SHARED_SECRET}" | awk '{print $NF}')" curl -X POST "${API_BASE}/events/poll" \ -H "Authorization: Bearer ${MEDEXPRESS_TOKEN}" \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -H "group-id: ${GROUP_ID}" \ -H "subscription-id: ${SUBSCRIPTION_ID}" \ -H "event-signature: ${POLL_SIGNATURE}" \ -d "${POLL_BODY}" DELIVERY_ID="<delivery-id-from-step-4>" POLL_BODY="{\"ack\": [\"${DELIVERY_ID}\"], \"maxEvents\": 20}" POLL_SIGNATURE="sha256=$(printf %s "${POLL_BODY}" | openssl dgst -sha256 -hmac "${SHARED_SECRET}" | awk '{print $NF}')" curl -X POST "${API_BASE}/events/poll" \ -H "Authorization: Bearer ${MEDEXPRESS_TOKEN}" \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -H "group-id: ${GROUP_ID}" \ -H "subscription-id: ${SUBSCRIPTION_ID}" \ -H "event-signature: ${POLL_SIGNATURE}" \ -d "${POLL_BODY}" $DeliveryId = "<delivery-id-from-step-4>" $PollBody = '{"ack": ["' + $DeliveryId + '"], "maxEvents": 20}' $Hmac = [System.Security.Cryptography.HMACSHA256]::new([Text.Encoding]::UTF8.GetBytes($env:SHARED_SECRET)) $PollSignature = 'sha256=' + [BitConverter]::ToString($Hmac.ComputeHash([Text.Encoding]::UTF8.GetBytes($PollBody))).Replace('-', '').ToLower() Invoke-RestMethod -Method Post -Uri "$env:API_BASE/events/poll" ` -Headers @{ Authorization = "Bearer $env:MEDEXPRESS_TOKEN" "group-id" = $env:GROUP_ID "subscription-id" = $env:SUBSCRIPTION_ID "event-signature" = $PollSignature } ` -ContentType "application/json" ` -Body $PollBody | ConvertTo-Json -Depth 10 An acknowledged event isn't returned again, so with nothing else pending, the response comes back empty: {"moreAvailable":false,"sets":{}} If the receiver couldn't process an event, report it in setErrs instead of ack. A delivery ID goes in one or the other, never both.

Back in the Consent Portal as Anika, open Event Notifications → Events and find the delivery.preferences.update event. Its delivery to the poll subscription now shows Acknowledged: When you're done, tidy up by deleting the subscription and deregistering the topic in the portal. Expected result: the published event is queued for the poll subscription, MedExpress picks it up on its first poll, and once it's acknowledged it no longer shows up in later polls. For the full request options, errors, and HMAC settings, see Register a poll subscription and Poll event deliveries.
